\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =xy,\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\sqrt{xy},\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2x}\text{ }i+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2y}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$

The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by

$$
\nabla [fg] = g \, \nabla\! f  + f \, \nabla\! g.
$$

Using the product rule shown above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =\sqrt{xy}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+xy(\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2x}\text{ }i+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2y}\text{ }j) \\  & =\sqrt{xy}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{xy}}{2}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j).\end{aligned}
$$

The function 

$$
f(x,y)= \dfrac{xy^3}{x+y}
$$

is continuous except when the denominator is zero. However, the point $(-1,2)$ does not cause the denominator to become zero, so we can calculate the limit by substituting  $(-1,2)$ into the function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (-1,2)}\frac{x{y}^{3}}{x+y} & =\frac{(-1)\cdot {2}^{3}}{(-1)+2} \\  & =\frac{-8}{1} \\  & =-8\end{aligned}
$$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac 0 0,$ as follows:

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,1)}} \dfrac{x^2y+xy^2}{x^2-y^2} = \dfrac{(-1)^2(1) + (-1)(1)^2}{(-1)^2 - (1)^2} = \dfrac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{xy(x+y)}{(x+y)(x-y)} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{xy}{(x-y)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{xy}{(x-y)} & =\frac{(-1)\cdot 1}{-1-1} \\  & =\frac{-1}{-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\dfrac{1}{2}.$
Given the function $f(x,y) = 6x^2+2y^2 - 2xy^2,$ find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (3,3).$

The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y) = k$ at the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be expressed as

$$
\nabla f(x_0,y_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0 \rangle  = 0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (3,3)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-2x{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-2x{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =(12x-2{y}^{2})\text{ }i+(4y-4xy)\text{ }j \\ ∇\,f(3,3) & =(12(3)-2(3)^{2})i+(4(3)-4(3)(3))j \\  & =18\,i-24\,j \\  & =⟨18,-24⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent to the level curve that passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)=(3,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(3,3)\cdot ⟨x-3,\,y-3⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨18,-24⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,\,y-3⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can leave our answer in this form. Or, if we want to leave our final answer in Cartesian form, we expand the dot product and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}18(x-3)-24(y-3) & =0 \\ 18x-24y+18 & =0 \\ 3x-4y+3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the plane curve $x^2-3xy+4y=2.$ Find a tangent vector to the curve at the point $(1,1).$

First, if we set $f(x,y) = x^2-3xy+4y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=2.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
\mathbf t(1,1) = f_y(1,1) \ \mathbf i - f_x(1,1) \ \mathbf j
$$

So, we calculate $\mathbf t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3xy+4y)\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3xy+4y)\text{ }j \\  & =(-3x+4)\text{ }i-(2x-3y)\text{ }j \\ t(1,1) & =(-3(1)+4)\text{ }i-(2(1)-3(1))\text{ }j \\  & =1\,i-(-1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $\mathbf i +\mathbf j,$ as shown in the diagram below.

At which points on the curve $6xy+3y^2 =7+ y - 3x^2$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{j}?$

First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy+3{y}^{2} & =7+y-3{x}^{2} \\ 6xy+3{y}^{2}-y+3{x}^{2} & =7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y) = 6xy+3y^2 - y + 3x^2 ,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=7.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
\mathbf t(x,y) = f_y(x,y) \ \mathbf i - f_x(x,y) \ \mathbf j
$$

So, we calculate $\mathbf t(x,y)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(6xy+3{y}^{2}-y+3{x}^{2})\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy+3{y}^{2}-y+3{x}^{2})\,j \\  & =(6x+6y-1)\,i-(6y+6x)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $\mathbf{j},$ we must have $\mathbf t \cdot \mathbf j = 0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ((6x+6y-1)\,i-(6y+6x)\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -6y-6x & =0 \\ y & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-x$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy+3{y}^{2} & =7+y-3{x}^{2} \\ 6x(-x)+3(-x)^{2} & =7+(-x)-3{x}^{2} \\ -6{x}^{2}+3{x}^{2} & =7-x-3{x}^{2} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, if $x=7,$ we get $y=-7$ and the corresponding point is $(7,-7).$

Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y) = x^2 + 2y^2 +x$ that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1, 1).$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1,1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,1).$  

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,j \\  & =(2x+0+1)\,i+(0+4y+0)\,j \\  & =(2x+1)\,i+4y\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(2(1)+1)\,i+4(1)\,j \\  & =3\,i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we want a unit normal vector, we normalize $\nabla f(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,1)}{‖∇f(1,1)‖} & =\frac{3\,i+4\,j}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$
Consider the plane curve $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1.$ Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0, 4).$

To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $$
\displaystyle f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16} - 1,
$$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(0,4).$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)j \\  & =\frac{2x}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{8}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,4) & =\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{(4)}{8}\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j \\  & =⟨0,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,4).$

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{x-{x}_{0}}=\frac{{v}_{y}}{{v}_{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{y}(x-{x}_{0}) & ={v}_{x}(y-{y}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(x-0) & =0(y-4) \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that the equation of the normal line to the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1$ at the point $(0,4)$ is $x=0.$

$\nabla f(2, 3, \sqrt 2).$   

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }k \\  & =(4x-y)\text{ }i-x\text{ }j-2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,3,\sqrt{2}) & =(4\cdot 2-3)\text{ }i-2\text{ }j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k \\  & =5i-2j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z) = \ln (x^2 - xy) - z,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}.\end{aligned}

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $$

$$

$$

$$

$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{2y}{x} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{3{y}^{2}}{x}.\end{aligned}

$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}-v,\,y(u,v,w)={u}^{2}+v,\,z(u,v,w)={e}^{w}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$

$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 & 0 \\ 2u & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {e}^{w}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 \\ 2u & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}(2u+2u) \\  & =4u{e}^{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$

The area of the required region is given by

$$

$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$

$$

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x+y=u$ and $x-y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{4}-x+y=0\,⟹\,(x+y)^{4}-(x-y)=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{4},\end{aligned}
$$

Now, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y &=u \\ x-y &=v\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,y=\frac{u-v}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this value into the equation of the given line yields:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\, & ⟹\,\frac{u-v}{2}=0\,⟹\,v=u\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &={u}^{4} \\ v &=u\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}^{3}(u-1) &=0 \\ v &=u.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,{u}^{4}\le v\le u\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(-2)^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

$$

$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,-2⟩,\end{aligned}

and

r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,6-3u-2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(6-3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(6-3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 0 & -2\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,2,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨3,\,2,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =4xy\,{|}_{x=u\,y=v\,z=6-3u-2v} \\  & =4uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 3\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}4xy\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4uv\sqrt{14}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{14}{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{14}{\int }_{0}^{2}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{2}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot 4\cdot 9 \\  & =36\sqrt{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Construct the vector field that has the stream function $\psi(x,y) = e^{x} \cos{y}.$

A function $\psi(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf F= P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ if the following equations hold:

$$
P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y},\qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}
$$

Computing the partial derivatives of the function $\psi(x,y),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{∂ψ}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y, \\ Q & =-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x} \\  & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field with the stream function $\psi(x,y) = e^{x} \cos{y}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y) & =P\,i+Q\,j \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,i-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following vector fields have a stream function?

I. $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = x^4y\,\mathbf{i} - 2x^3y^2\,\mathbf{j}$

II. $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \sin x \sin y\,\mathbf{i} + \cos x \cos y\,\mathbf{j}$

III. $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = 4x^2y\,\mathbf{i} -4x^2y^2\,\mathbf{j}$

A vector field $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ with a simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ has a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field I has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4{x}^{3}y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-4{x}^{3}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
= 4x^3y + (- 4x^3y)
= 0
$$

- Vector field II has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
= \cos x \sin y + (- \cos x \sin y)
= 0.
$$

- Vector field III doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=8xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-8{x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
= 8xy + (- 8x^2y)
\neq 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."
Determine the equation of the streamline that passes through the point $P(-1,1)$ for the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (x^3-3xy^2)\,\mathbf{i} + (y^3-3x^2y)\,\mathbf{j}.$

The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.

A vector field $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ with a simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ has a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.
$$

Note that $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (x^3-3xy^2)\,\mathbf{i} + (y^3-3x^2y)\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D=\mathbb{R}^2,$ where $P(x,y) = x^3-3xy^2$ and $Q(x,y) = y^3 - 3x^2y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =3{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\mathbf F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = (3x^2-3y^2) + (3y^2 - 3x^2) = 0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $\psi(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf F= P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ if 

$$
P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} = x^3-3xy^2, \qquad \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} = -y^3+3x^2y.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
\psi(x,y) = x^3y - xy^3 + f(x), \qquad 
\psi(x,y) = -xy^3 + x^3y + g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
\psi(x,y) = x^3y - xy^3.
$$

Finally, we find the level curve of the stream function $\psi(x,y) = x^3y - xy^3$ that passes through $P.$
First, we find the value of the stream function at $P{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(-1,1) & =(-1)^{3}(1)-(-1)(1)^{3} \\  & =-1-(-1) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the streamline that passes through $P(-1,1)$ is the $0$-level curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =0 \\ {x}^{3}y-x{y}^{3} & =0 \\ xy({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ xy(x+y)(x-y) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our possible streamlines are $x=0,$ $y=0,$ $y=-x,$ or $y=x.$ The streamline that passes through $P(-1,1)$ is $y=-x.$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $\psi(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf F= P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ if

If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C\mathbin:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

The outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. From the diagram below we see that $\mathbf F$ acts perpendicular to $\mathbf n$ at every point on $C.$ Therefore, there is no net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

![](images/4a/4a3d9864bb6bada1fd218b299427bc5bb4ffcbcccb1a504fff77416d5d292151.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

- Statement III is false. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/93/9310d17389f61de2984c0e23cfe1060e77d4a87a140d2f1c892bdbab9b99629b.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
\oint\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

$$

=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

$$

$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_1,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \mathbf i + t\,\mathbf j, \quad \Rightarrow\quad \mathbf r'(t) = \mathbf j, \qquad t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =2(1-(-1)) \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}

$$

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i-2xy\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=-2xy.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2x+(-2x)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if

$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{x}{5} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{y}{4} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

$$

x=x(t)={t}^{2}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le \sqrt{6}
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le \sqrt{6}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2t\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{12x}{y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{12{t}^{2}}{t} \\  & =12t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{12x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{6}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{6}}12t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=4{t}^{2}+1,$ $\text{d}u=8t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{6}}12t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t & =12{\int }_{5}^{25}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{5}^{25}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,{|}_{5}^{25} \\  & =\sqrt{{25}^{3}}-\sqrt{{5}^{3}} \\  & =125-5\sqrt{5} \\  & =5(25-\sqrt{5})\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,1)$ to $(1,2).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+j$ and $b=i+2\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-i+j)+t[(i+2\,j)-(-i+j)] \\  & =(-i+j)+t(2\,i+j) \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2t-1$ and $y=t+1$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)j \\  & =2\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

A connected region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ can be contracted to a point.

![](images/7d/7d6aea1a62fb290702630ef95ec86f4119e7c8fdd74b8148b62b66e5ac871b58.png)

A connected *plane* region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ encloses only points in $D.$ In other words, the region does not contain any holes. Plane regions containing holes are not simply connected, since some simple closed curves cannot be contracted to a point:

![](images/c3/c3c3e7a60ff0dd917cf6c0b293dae7510e457a0455629add1c54cadac65248b7.png)

Let's now examine our regions in turn.

- Region ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1}$ is *not* simply connected. The region contains all the points of ${R}^{2}$ except those on the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ Thus, the region is formed by two disjoint pieces and, therefore, is not even a connected region.

- Region ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,(x,y)\ne (0,0)}$ is *not* simply connected since it's a plane region with a hole at $(0,0).$

- Region ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,x\ge 0}$ is simply connected. It's a plane region without holes.

Therefore, the correct answer is ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,x\ge 0}$ only.

We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a half of a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =4{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}[(1)^{3}-(-1)^{3}] \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$

$$

$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(1,2)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$

$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x-1}+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\sqrt{(1+t)-1}+2-t \\  & =\sqrt{t}-t+2.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{t}-t+2)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{1/2}-t+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+2t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+2)-(0) \\  & =\frac{13}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following regions are simply connected?

Select all that apply.

A connected region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ can be contracted to a point.

![](images/7d/7d6aea1a62fb290702630ef95ec86f4119e7c8fdd74b8148b62b66e5ac871b58.png)

A connected *plane* region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ encloses only points in $D.$ In other words, the region does not contain any holes. Plane regions containing holes are not simply connected, since some simple closed curves cannot be contracted to a point:

![](images/c3/c3c3e7a60ff0dd917cf6c0b293dae7510e457a0455629add1c54cadac65248b7.png)

Let's now examine our regions in turn.

- Region ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,y-x\ge 0}$ is simply connected. Indeed, it is the half-plane $y\ge x.$ So,   it's a plane region without holes,

- Region ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1}$ is *not* simply connected since it's a plane region with a hole (containing all points of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1$).

- Region ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,y+x\ne 0}$ is *not* simply connected. The region contains all the points of ${R}^{2}$ except those on the straight line $y=-x.$ Thus, the region is formed by two disjoint half-planes and, therefore, is not even a connected region.

Therefore, the correct answer is ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,y-x\ge 0}$ only.

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\displaystyle \int x{e}^{-3x}\text{d}x$ as $\displaystyle \int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-3x}\, & ⟹\,v=-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \left(-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}\right)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{x{e}^{-3x}}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{x{e}^{-3x}}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{9}+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u=3x+5\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=3 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-5x}\, & ⟹\,v=-\frac{{e}^{-5x}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (3x+5)\cdot {e}^{-5x}\,\text{d}x & =(3x+5)\cdot \left(-\frac{{e}^{-5x}}{5}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{{e}^{-5x}}{5}\right)\cdot 3\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F=x\,i+y\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/3b/3bd953b7fb02b90a55a29bea6f58ff9bd8bab77d62b1df1c547ca899656d37a3.png)

First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(x\,i+y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=2\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =2(2-(-2)) \\  & =2\cdot 4 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides ${C}_{2},{C}_{3},$ and ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=4\cdot 8=32.
$$

$$

\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\, &  & ∇f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,i+2xy{z}^{3}\,j+3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,k, &  &  \\ h(x,y,z) & =\frac{1}{xyz},\, &  & ∇h(x,y,z)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}z}\,j-\frac{1}{xy{z}^{2}}\text{ }k. &  & \end{aligned}
$$

The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=h∇f+f∇h.
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)] & =h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z)+f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{1}{xyz}({y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,i+2xy{z}^{3}\,j+3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,k)+x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}z}\,j-\frac{1}{xy{z}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{xyz}\,i+\frac{2xy{z}^{3}}{xyz}\,j+\frac{3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}{xyz}\,k-\frac{x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}z}\,j-\frac{x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{xy{z}^{2}}\,k \\  & =\frac{y{z}^{2}}{x}\,i+2{z}^{2}\,j+3yz\,k-\frac{y{z}^{2}}{x}\,i-{z}^{2}\,j-yz\,k \\  & ={z}^{2}\,j+2yz\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

The function $f(x,y)$ is continuous except when the denominator is zero. However, the point $(0,-1)$ does not cause the denominator to vanish, so we can calculate the limit by substituting $(0,-1)$ into the function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,-1)}\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =\frac{{0}^{2}-(-1)^{2}}{{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0-1}{0+1} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Given the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1),$ find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-1,0).$

The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1))\,j \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\,i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\,j \\ ∇f(-1,0) & =\frac{2(-1)}{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+1}\,i+\frac{2(0)}{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+1}\,j \\  & =(-1)i+0\,j \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(-1,0)\cdot ⟨x-(-1),\,y-0⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨-1,0⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the plane curve $x\operatorname{cos}⁡y=-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0).$

First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{\pi }{2} \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(\frac{\pi }{2},0)={f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},0)i-{f}_{x}(\frac{\pi }{2},0)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)j \\  & =(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)j \\ t(\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =(-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡0+\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right))i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡0+0\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right))j \\  & =i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $i-j.$

At which point on the curve ${x}^{2}y=-8x-4$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $j?$

First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y & =-8x-4 \\ {x}^{2}y+8x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y+8x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-4.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y+8x)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y+8x)\,j \\  & ={x}^{2}\,i-(2xy+8)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j,$ we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}\,i-(2xy+8)\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -(2xy+8) & =0 \\ xy+4 & =0 \\ y & =-\frac{4}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-\frac{4}{x}$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y & =-8x-4 \\ {x}^{2}\left(-\frac{4}{x}\right) & =-8x-4 \\ -4x & =-8x-4 \\ 4x & =-4 \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $x=-1,$ we get $y=4,$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,4).$
Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{y}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,4).$

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{y})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{y})\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,j \\ ∇f(1,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1}}\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{1}{2}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,4)}{‖∇f(1,4)‖} & =\frac{\frac{1}{2}(i+j)}{‖\frac{1}{2}(i+j)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}})}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j).\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the determinant of
$$

$$
is $-48$, find all the possible values of $z.$

$$

$$

Since the determinant of the matrix is $-48,$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}-13z-6 & =-48 \\ {z}^{2}-13z+42 & =0 \\ z & =\frac{-(-13)\pm \sqrt{{13}^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 42}}{2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{13\pm \sqrt{1}}{2} \\  & =\frac{13\pm 1}{2} \\  & =6,7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $z=6$ and $z=7.$

$$

To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{x}{5} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{y}{3} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

 
Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1.

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\pi /6 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡v-0\cdot 0 \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\pi /6 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(\frac{\pi }{6},0)}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u+v,\,u,\,v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & ={x}^{2}-2yz\,{|}_{x=u+v\,y=u\,z=v} \\  & =(u+v)^{2}-2uv \\  & ={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\},
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-2yz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}+{v}^{2})\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u{v}^{2}]}_{u=-1}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{[\frac{2}{3}v+\frac{2}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

and

what is the value of $a+b+c?$

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}+2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{3}+3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2u,\,3{u}^{2}⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}+2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{3}+3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2,\,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 2u & 3{u}^{2} \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}2u & 3{u}^{2} \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3{u}^{2} \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2u \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨6u-6{u}^{2},\,3{u}^{2}-3,\,2-2u⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩{|}_{x=u+v\,y={u}^{2}+2v\,z={u}^{3}+3v} \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩\cdot ⟨6u-6{u}^{2},\,3{u}^{2}-3,\,2-2u⟩ \\  & =1\cdot (6u-6{u}^{2})+0\cdot (3{u}^{2}-3)+2\cdot (2-2u) \\  & =6u-6{u}^{2}+4-4u \\  & =-6{u}^{2}+2u+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-6)\cdot {u}^{2}+2\cdot u+4\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=-6+2+4=0.
$$

Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+x\,j$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+0\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2}]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=y\,i-x\,j+z\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,j+{t}^{2}\,k$ for $t\in [-\pi ,\pi ).$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,z={t}^{2}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i-x\,j+z\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j+{t}^{2}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j+{t}^{2}\,k)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j+2t\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))+{t}^{2}\cdot 2t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+2{t}^{3} \\  & =1+2{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(1+2{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[t+\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =((\pi -(-\pi ))+\frac{{\pi }^{4}-(-\pi )^{4}}{2}) \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2{t}^{3}-2t,\,y=3{t}^{2}+3t,\,z={t}^{3}-t.
$$

So,

$$

$$

$$

Let $g=\begin{bmatrix}{r}^{2} \\ -1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}$ and $h=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ {r}^{2} \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Given that $g⊥h$ and $r<0$, find the value of $r.$

We know that $g⊥h$ ($g$ and $h$ are perpendicular) if and only if $g\cdot h=0.$

Computing the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}g\cdot h & ={g}_{x}\cdot {h}_{x}+{g}_{y}\cdot {h}_{y}+{g}_{z}\cdot {h}_{z} \\  & ={r}^{2}\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot {r}^{2}+(-6)\cdot 2 \\  & =3{r}^{2}-{r}^{2}-12 \\  & =2{r}^{2}-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}g\cdot h & =0 \\ 2{r}^{2}-12 & =0 \\ 2{r}^{2} & =12 \\ {r}^{2} & =6 \\ r & =\pm \sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F=2x\,i+2y\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $8$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across all four sides of the square.*

If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/0b/0b753318ebad9270c3fc8788d0e3949ffb29a800eb3f8dd6fb67cb271be68033.png)

First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(2x\,i+2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=4\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-4,4].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =2{\int }_{-4}^{4}4\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{-4}^{4}\text{d}t \\  & =8(4-(-4)) \\  & =8\cdot 8 \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides ${C}_{2},{C}_{3},$ and ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=4\cdot 64=256.
$$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*

If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/f2/f283fe675e0a9ef736947e404f03ab5afb90a4209ba1a6949d18ac6d3fb20048.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(x\,i+3y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=3\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-3,3].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-3}^{3}3\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{-3}^{3}\text{d}t \\  & =3\cdot 6 \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=18.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(x\,i+3y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+3\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-3,3].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =3{\int }_{-3}^{3}3\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{-3}^{3}\text{d}t \\  & =9\cdot 6 \\  & =54.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=54.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot 18+2\cdot 54=144.
$$

$$

$$

$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement “The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=x$” is false. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\frac{2y+x}{3x+y} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{2x+x}{3x+x} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{3x}{4x} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\,\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The limit evaluates to $-\frac{1}{2}$ along the path $y=-x$” is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=-x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=-x}\frac{2y+x}{3x+y} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{-2x+x}{3x-x} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{-x}{2x} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The limit exists and is equal to $0$” is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{2y+x}{3x+y}=\text{DNE}
$$

Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$, can be found by computing $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j \\ ∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}) & =2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\text{ }i+2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\text{ }j \\  & =-i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})}{‖∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})‖} & =\frac{-i+j}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-i+j}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation 
$\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1?$

Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=16$ and ${b}^{2}=9.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=16,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be  $a=\sqrt{16}=4.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=9,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{9}=3.$

So the semi-major axis has length $a=4,$ and the semi-minor axis has length $b=3.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2a=2\cdot 4=8,$ and the minor axis has length $2b=2\cdot 3=6.$

Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the line segment from $(1,2)$ to $(4,7).$

We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,2)$ to $(4,7).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+2\,j$ and $b=4\,i+7j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(i+2\,j)+t[4\,i+7j-(i+2\,j)] \\  & =(i+2\,j)+t(3i+5j) \\  & =(1+3t)\,i+(2+5t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1+3t$ and $y=2+5t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+5t)j \\  & =3i+5j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{34}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+3t)(2+5t) \\  & =15{t}^{2}+11t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(15{t}^{2}+11t+2)\cdot \sqrt{34}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{34}{\int }_{0}^{1}(15{t}^{2}+11t+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{34}{[5{t}^{3}+\frac{11}{2}{t}^{2}+2t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{34}(5+\frac{11}{2}+2)-0 \\  & =\frac{25\sqrt{34}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that $u⊥v$ ($u$ and $v$ are perpendicular) if and only if $u\cdot v=0.$

Computing the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot v & ={u}_{x}\cdot {v}_{x}+{u}_{y}\cdot {v}_{y}+{u}_{z}\cdot {v}_{z} \\  & =a\cdot a+2\cdot (-4)+4\cdot (-2) \\  & ={a}^{2}-16.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot v & =0 \\ {a}^{2}-16 & =0 \\ {a}^{2} & =16 \\ a & =\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=1-t$ and $y=1-t.$ Therefore, 

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -5 \\ \frac{x+5}{3} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+5)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+5)^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2 \\ \frac{y+2}{6} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+2)^{2}}{{6}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+2)^{2}}{36} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $$

Given a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v).$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v) & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)\, & \operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v).\end{aligned}

$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 2x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =2x\cdot \left(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}\right)\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$

$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 \\ 0 & -3\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot (-3\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-0\cdot 0 \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x},$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1).$

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(0,0,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x})\,k \\  & =({e}^{y}+z{e}^{x})\,i+(x{e}^{y}+{e}^{z})\,j+(y{e}^{z}+{e}^{x})\,k \\ ∇f(0,0,1) & =({e}^{0}+(1){e}^{0})i+((0){e}^{0}+{e}^{1})j+((0){e}^{1}+{e}^{0})k \\  & =2\,i+e\,j+k\end{aligned}

Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the following curves and lines.

$$
y=\frac{2}{{x}^{2}},\,y=\frac{4}{{x}^{2}},\,y=\frac{1}{x},\,y=\frac{3}{x}
$$

The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

We'll assume this transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv,
$$

  

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required area, we proceed in five steps:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
{x}^{2}y=2,\,{x}^{2}y=4,\,xy=1,\,xy=3
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u={x}^{2}y,\,v=xy
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u={x}^{2}y$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{2}y=2\,⟹\,u=2 \\  & {x}^{2}y=4\,⟹\,u=4\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=xy$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & xy=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & xy=3\,⟹\,v=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 4,\,1\le v\le 3\}
$$

![](images/ba/baa8e8ab6cff8edec84d3f0d0950931f247153523e3320abbdf673161afb44ae.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2xy & {x}^{2} \\ y & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}y \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨y,\,2yz,\,-{z}^{2}+1⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the half-cone $z=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and the plane $z=-3.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the half-cone $z=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and the plane $z=-3.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=-3.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3)=0 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,2yz,\,-{z}^{2}+1⟩{|}_{z=-3} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{y}_{P},\,\underbrace{-6y}_{Q},\,\underbrace{-8}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot 0-(-6y)\cdot 0-8)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-8\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ with radius $3$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-8\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}-8\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =-8[\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{r=0}^{r=3} \\  & =-8(2\pi -0)\cdot (\frac{9}{2}-0) \\  & =-72\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,
$$

where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨-y,\,z,\,-2x⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=2+2x-y.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=2+2x-y.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=2+2x-y.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2+2x-y)=2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2+2x-y)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-y,\,z,\,-2x⟩{|}_{z=2+2x-y} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{-y}_{P},\,\underbrace{2+2x-y}_{Q},\,\underbrace{-2x}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-y)\cdot (2)-(2+2x-y)\cdot (-1)-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y+2+2x-y-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2+y)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$

$$

 

we obtain

$$

$$

$$

$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x-y,\,v=y+1
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x-y=u$ and $y=v+1$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-y)^{2}+y=2\,⟹\,(y+1)=3-(x-y)^{2}\,⟹\,v=3-{u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

 

while substituting $y=v-1$ into the equation of the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &=3-{u}^{2} \\ v &=1\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}u &=\pm \sqrt{2} \\ v &=1.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm \sqrt{2},1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,-\sqrt{2}\le u\le \sqrt{2},\,1\le v\le 3-{u}^{2}.}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=\frac{1}{u},\,y(u,v,w)={v}^{2}+w,\,z(u,v,w)=vw.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-\frac{1}{{u}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =w & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{1}{{u}^{2}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2v & 1 \\ 0 & w & v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\begin{vmatrix}2v & 1 \\ w & v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}(2{v}^{2}-w).\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Given that $g(x,y)=4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇g(x,y)=0.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4y+0-2x \\  & =2(2y-x) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4x+2y-0 \\  & =2(2x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇g(x,y)=2(2y-x)\,i+2(2x+y)\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇g(x,y)=0:$

$$
2(2y-x)\,i+2(2x+y)\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2y-x &=0 \\ 2x+y &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=2y.$ Substituting these into the second equation, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2y)+y & =0 \\ 5y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get $x=2\cdot 0=0.$

Therefore, $∇g(x,y)=0$ at the point $(0,0).$
Given that $g(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z$, find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $∇g(x,y,z)=0.$

First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{1}{x}+0+0-1-0-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =0+\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\cdot \frac{1}{y}+0-0-1-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =0+0+\operatorname{ln}⁡z+z\cdot \frac{1}{z}-0-0-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇g(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,k.$ 

Now, we solve $∇g(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficient of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x &=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y &=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=1.$  Similarly, from the second and third equations, we obtain $y=1$ and $z=1.$

Hence, $∇g(x,y,z)=0$ at the point $(1,1,1).$

Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have 

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{2}{t}.
$$

 

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{2}{t},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le 6
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 6$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{2}{t}\right)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\left(-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}\right)}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{{t}^{4}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4+{t}^{4}}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=4x{y}^{2},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4\left(\frac{2}{t}\right)(t)^{2} \\  & =8t.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y},$ traversed along the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(-3,4)?$

We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(-3,4).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=0$ and $b=-3\,i+4\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =0+t\,(b-0) \\  & =t(b) \\  & =t(-3\,i+4\,j) \\  & =-3t\,i+4t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-3t$ and $y=4t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)j \\  & =-3\,i+4\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={e}^{-3t+4t} \\  & ={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\cdot 5\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(3,-2,3)$ to $(5,-1,7).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=3i-2\,j+3k$ and $b=5\,i-j+7\,k.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(3i-2\,j+3k)+t[(5\,i-j+7\,k)-(3i-2\,j+3k)] \\  & =(3i-2\,j+3k)+t(2i+\,j+4k) \\  & =(2t+3)\,i+(t-2)\,j+(4t+3)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2t+3,y=t-2,$ and $z=4t+3$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$

$$

The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-x+y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-x+y)\,j \\  & =({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }i+(2xy+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(1,-1) & =((-1)^{2}-1)\,i+(2(1)(-1)+1)\,j \\  & =0\,i-j \\  & =⟨0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-(-1)⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨0,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y+1⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2} & =y+1 \\ 2{x}^{2}-y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-y)\,j \\  & =-i-4x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i+j,$ we must have $t\cdot (i+j)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot (i+j) & =0 \\ (-i-4x\,j)\cdot (i+j) & =0 \\ -1-4x & =0 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$

$$

What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation 
$\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{18}=1?$

Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=9$ and ${b}^{2}=18.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=9,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{9}=3.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=18,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{18}=3\sqrt{2}.$

So the semi-major axis has length $b=3\sqrt{2},$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=3.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot 3\sqrt{2}=6\sqrt{2},$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot 3=6.$
