For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-1).$

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,-1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z)\,k \\  & =3{x}^{2}\text{ }i+2{z}^{2}y\text{ }j+(2z{y}^{2}+2)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,-1) & =3(1)^{2}\,i+2(-1)^{2}(-1)\,j+(2(-1)(-1)^{2}+2)k \\  & =3\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $3\,i-2\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-1).$

Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v),$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨3x,\,3y,\,z⟩,\,r(u,v)=⟨u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,{u}^{2}⟩,\,(u,v)\in D⊂{R}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,u⟩.$*

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Notice we are told that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,u⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨3x,\,3y,\,z⟩{|}_{x=u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,y=u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\,z={u}^{2}} \\  & =⟨3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,{u}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,{u}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,u⟩ \\  & =3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot (-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v)+3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot (-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v)+{u}^{2}\cdot u \\  & =-6{u}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v)+{u}^{3} \\  & =-5{u}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,-5{u}^{3}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v),$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨xz,\,y,\,xz⟩,\,r(u,v)=⟨u,\,uv,\,v⟩,\,(u,v)\in D⊂{R}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨v,\,-1,\,u⟩.$*

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Notice we are told that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨v,\,-1,\,u⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨xz,\,y,\,xz⟩{|}_{x=u\,y=uv\,z=v} \\  & =⟨uv,\,uv,\,uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨uv,\,uv,\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨v,\,-1,\,u⟩ \\  & =uv\cdot v+uv\cdot (-1)+uv\cdot u \\  & =u{v}^{2}-uv+{u}^{2}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,u{v}^{2}-uv+{u}^{2}v\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$
For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1).$

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-1,0,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,0,1) & =2(-1)\,i+2(0)\,j+2(1)\,k \\  & =-2\,i+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-2\,i+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1).$
For the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0).$

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(0,0,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z)\,k \\  & =({e}^{x+y+z}+1)\text{ }i+({e}^{x+y+z}+1)\text{ }j+({e}^{x+y+z}+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,0,0) & =({e}^{0+0+0}+1)\,i+({e}^{0+0+0}+1)\,j+({e}^{0+0+0}+1)\,k \\  & =2\,i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $2\,i+2\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0).$

What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation 
$$
\displaystyle \frac{{x}^{2}}{49}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{36}=1?
$$

Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=49$ and ${b}^{2}=36.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=49,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{49}=7.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=36,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{36}=6.$

Thus, the semi-major axis has length $a=7,$ and the semi-minor axis has length $b=6.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2a=2\cdot 7=14,$ and the minor axis has length $2b=2\cdot 6=12.$

Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $F$ given below?

Select all that apply.

$$
F=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 8 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(F) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 8 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}-8\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 5 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(2-3)-8(-1-5)+3(-3-10) \\  & =2\cdot (-1)-8\cdot (-6)+3\cdot (-13) \\  & =-2+48-39 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(F)=7$, the matrix is **not** singular. 

Therefore, only statement “$F$ is **not** a singular matrix” is true.

Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $S$ given below?

$$

$$

Given that the determinant of
$$
\displaystyle \begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & m \\ m & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$
is $-29$, find all the possible values of $m.$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.

Let's use our formula to find an expression for the determinant in terms of $m:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 6 & m \\ m & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & =1\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}-6\begin{vmatrix}m & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}+m\begin{vmatrix}m & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(3-0)-6(m-0)+m(m-6) \\  & =3-6m+{m}^{2}-6m \\  & ={m}^{2}-12m+3\end{aligned}
$$

Since the determinant of the matrix is $-29,$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12m+3 & =-29 \\ {m}^{2}-12m+32 & =0 \\ m & =\frac{-(-12)\pm \sqrt{{12}^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 32}}{2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{12\pm \sqrt{16}}{2} \\  & =\frac{12\pm 4}{2} \\  & =6\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $m=4$ and $m=8.$

Given that $g(x,y)=\frac{9}{y}-\frac{3y}{x}+x,$ find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇g(x,y)=0.$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{9}{y}-\frac{3y}{x}+x) \\  & =\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}+1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{9}{y}-\frac{3y}{x}+x) \\  & =-\frac{9}{{y}^{2}}-\frac{3}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $$
\displaystyle ∇g(x,y)=(\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}+1)i-(\frac{9}{{y}^{2}}+\frac{3}{x})j.
$$

Now, we solve $∇g(x,y)=0:$

$$
(\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}+1)i-(\frac{9}{{y}^{2}}+\frac{3}{x})j=0\,i+0\,j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{cases}\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}+1=0 \\ \frac{9}{{y}^{2}}+\frac{3}{x}=0\end{cases}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{{\left(-\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}\right)}^{2}}+\frac{3}{x} & =0 \\ 9\cdot {\left(-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\right)}^{2}+\frac{3}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{81}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{3}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{81+3{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}} & =0 \\ 81+3{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =-27 \\ x & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=-3,$ we get $y=-\frac{(-3)^{2}}{3}=-3.$

Therefore, $∇g(x,y)=0$ at the point: $(-3,-3).$

At which points on the curve ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2y-2x$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $-i+j?$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.

First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2y-2x \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-2y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-2y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-2y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-2y)\,j \\  & =(2y-2)\,i-(2x+2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $-i+j,$ we must have $t\cdot (-i+j)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot (-i+j) & =0 \\ ((2y-2)\,i-(2x+2)\,j)\cdot (-i+j) & =0 \\ -(2y-2)-(2x+2) & =0 \\ -2y-2x & =0 \\ y & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-x$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2y-2x \\ {x}^{2}+(-x)^{2} & =2(-x)-2x \\ 2{x}^{2} & =-4x \\ 2{x}^{2}+4x & =0 \\ 2x(x+2) & =0 \\ x & =-2,0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- For $x=-2,$ we get $y=2,$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,2).$

- For $x=0,$ we get $y=0,$ and the corresponding point is $(0,0).$

Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}u+2w \\ v-u \\ uw\end{bmatrix}.
$$

For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+2w,\,y(u,v,w)=v-u,\,z(u,v,w)=uw.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =2 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =w & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ w & 0 & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & u\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ w & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(u-0)+2(0-w) \\  & =u-2w.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ u-2w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u-2w=0$ defines the plane $u=2w.$
The critical points lie on the $vw-$plane.
The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $w=-2{v}^{2}.$
The critical points lie on the plane $2u+v+w=0.$
The critical points lie on the plane $w=-2u.$
The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $w={u}^{2}.$

Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{u} \\ {e}^{u+w} \\ uv+w\end{bmatrix}.
$$

For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={e}^{u},\,y(u,v,w)={e}^{u+w},\,z(u,v,w)=uv+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+w} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & ={e}^{u+w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{u} & 0 & 0 \\ {e}^{u+w} & 0 & {e}^{u+w} \\ v & u & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u}\begin{vmatrix}0 & {e}^{u+w} \\ u & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u}(0-u{e}^{u+w}) \\  & =-u{e}^{2u+w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ -u{e}^{2u+w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u=0$ defines the plane $u=0,$ i.e., $vw$-plane.

Consider the finite region $R$ in the $xyz$-space, given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x+3y\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le z-3y\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le z\le 2}.
$$

Given the change of variables

$$
u=x+3y,\,v=z-3y,\,w=z,
$$

which of the following could be the missing part of the expression below?

$$
{∭}_{R}{cos}^{2}⁡(x+z)\operatorname{cos}⁡(z-3y)\,dV={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,dw\,dv\,du
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+3y,\,v=z-3y,\,w=z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le u\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le w\le 2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-3-0) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{cos}^{2}⁡(x+z)\operatorname{cos}⁡(z-3y)\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}{cos}^{2}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot |\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}{cos}^{2}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot |-\frac{1}{3}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\frac{1}{3}{cos}^{2}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,\,dw\,dv\,du\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is a stream function for the vector field
$F(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y\,i-2x{y}^{2}\,j?$

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y\,i-2x{y}^{2}\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=-2x{y}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=4xy+(-4xy)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y,\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}=(xy)^{2}.
$$

What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation 
$\frac{{x}^{2}}{1}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{8}=1?$

Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=1$ and ${b}^{2}=8.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=1,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{1}=1.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=8,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}.$

So the semi-major axis has length $b=2\sqrt{2},$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=1.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot 2\sqrt{2}=4\sqrt{2},$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot 1=2.$

Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $z=2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$

First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x \\ z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(\frac{1}{2},1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)k \\  & =(-4x-1)\text{ }i-4y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3) & =(-4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-1)\,i-4(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =-3\,i-4\,j+k \\  & =⟨-3,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ and passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Given that $$
\displaystyle f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z,
$$ find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $∇f(x,y,z)=0.$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.

First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}+0-\frac{1}{z{x}^{2}}-0 \\  & =-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}+0-0 \\  & =-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =0+0-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}x}-1 \\  & =-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $$
\displaystyle ∇f(x,y,z)=-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}\,j-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\,k.
$$ 

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}\,j-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficient of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{cases}-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}=0 \\ -\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}=0 \\ -\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}=0\end{cases}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x=-1.$ Substituting these into the third equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x} & =0 \\ -\frac{1+{z}^{2}(-1)}{{z}^{2}(-1)} & =0 \\ 1-{z}^{2} & =0 \\ {z}^{2} & =1 \\ z & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-1$ into the first equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{(-1)^{2}yz} & =0 \\ z+y & =0 \\ y & =-z\end{aligned}
$$

When $z=1,$ we have $y=-1$ and when $z=-1,$ we have $y=1.$

Hence, $∇f(x,y,z)=0$ at two points: $(-1,-1,1)$ and $(-1,1,-1).$
At which points on the curve ${y}^{2}-4xy=-5{x}^{2}+1$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$

First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4xy & =-5{x}^{2}+1 \\ {y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2})j \\  & =2(y-2x)\,i-(10x-4y)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ (2(y-2x)\,i-(10x-4y)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2(y-2x) & =0 \\ y & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=2x$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ (2x)^{2}-4x(2x)+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ 4{x}^{2}-8{x}^{2}+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=1$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(1,2).$

- If $x=-1$, we get $y=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,-2).$

Using the change of variables 

$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the lines $x+y=1,$ $x-y=1$ and the curve ${x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=2.$

The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x-y,\,v=x+y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x+y=v$ into the equation of the first line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y=1\,⟹\,v=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x-y=u$ into the equation of the second line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y=1\,⟹\,u=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x+y=v$ and $x-y=u$ into the equation of curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=2\,⟹\,(x-y)(x+y)=2,\,⟹\,uv=2.\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection point of the two lines in the $uv$-plane is $(1,1).$

To find the intersection of the curve with the first line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}uv &=2 \\ v &=1\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}u &=2 \\ v &=1.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the intersections of the curve with the second line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}uv &=2 \\ u &=1\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}u &=1 \\ v &=2.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the intersection points are $(1,1),$ $(1,2)$ and $(2,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le \frac{2}{u}\}.
$$

![](images/4c/4c151e7fc8d150b9c8def69d609446b77424c2703decd9c8c55866cff2ae7437.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(2)^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{2/u}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}[v]_{1}^{2/u}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{2}{u}-1)du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[2\operatorname{ln}⁡u-u]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-1) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/09/0950c559d5d6df93cf40afd8fdbd07f090f864fa462083bfd496246e7f2bded9.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(3x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =3{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=2i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-3,3].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =3{\int }_{-3}^{3}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{-3}^{3}\text{d}t \\  & =6\cdot 6 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=36.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(3x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =-2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+3j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-2{\int }_{-2}^{2}3\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =(-6)\cdot 4 \\  & =-24.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=-24.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot 36+2\cdot (-24)=24.
$$

If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/eb/ebe05a522f9f46acfed63e29927b46f41d78483b5df5e7a15a15ae5f33abd2f4.png)

First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-4x\,i-4y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-4{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =-4(1-(-1)) \\  & =(-4)\cdot 2 \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides ${C}_{2},{C}_{3},$ and ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=4\cdot (-8)=-32.
$$

If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-x\,i+2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=2\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-{\int }_{-2}^{2}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =-2\cdot 4 \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=-8.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(-x\,i+2y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+2\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =2{\int }_{-2}^{2}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot 4 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=16.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot (-8)+2\cdot 16=16.
$$

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}2uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,2v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2v \\ 0 & 1 & 2u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2v \\ 1 & 2u\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2v \\ 0 & 2u\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-2v,\,-2u,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨{x}^{2},\,xy,\,z⟩{|}_{x=u\,y=v\,z=2uv} \\  & =⟨{u}^{2},\,uv,\,2uv⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨{u}^{2},\,uv,\,2uv⟩\cdot ⟨-2v,\,-2u,\,1⟩ \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot (-2v)+uv\cdot (-2u)+2uv\cdot 1 \\  & =-2{u}^{2}v-2{u}^{2}v+2uv \\  & =2uv-4{u}^{2}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\cdot uv+(-4)\cdot {u}^{2}v\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=2-4=-2.
$$

$$

Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$

$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $y,z\ne 0.$*

For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=\frac{z}{y},\,v(x,y,z)=y,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-\frac{z}{{y}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & -\frac{z}{{y}^{2}} & \frac{1}{y} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =z\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{z}{{y}^{2}} & \frac{1}{y} \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =z(0-\frac{1}{y}) \\  & =-\frac{z}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z}{y} & =-u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-u)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{8}{3},

\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$

We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the section of the curve $y=-\sqrt{x}$ from $O$ to $A.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t)=t\,i-\sqrt{t}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 4.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y=-\sqrt{t}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =t\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\sqrt{t})j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,j\end{aligned}

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,j) \\  & =t-\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2}\end{aligned}

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+\frac{8}{3} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(t-\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2})\text{d}t+\frac{8}{3} \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{t}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{0}^{4}+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{4}^{3/2}}{3}-0)+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=-y\,i+x\,j$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2\,k$ for $t\in [0,2).$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=2.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =-y\,i+x\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)\,k \\  & =-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j)\cdot (-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+0\,k) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+0\cdot 0 \\  & =2\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+2\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2\pi \,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi [t]_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\pi (2-0) \\  & =4\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate

where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨x+y,\,-x+y,\,-2z⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(x-1) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x+y,\,-x+y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{x+y}_{P},\,\underbrace{-x+y}_{Q},\,\underbrace{-2(x-1)^{2}-2(y+1)^{2}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(x+y)\cdot 2(x-1)-(-x+y)\cdot 2(y+1)-2((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2((x+y)(1-x)+(x-y)(y+1)-(x-1)^{2}-(y+1)^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4(-{r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\cdot r\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{r}^{3}+2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{[-{r}^{3}\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2\pi {r}^{3}-2\pi r)\,\text{d}r \\  & =-8\pi {[-\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-8\pi (-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y)h(x,y)$ if $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$ and $h(x,y)=y{e}^{x}?$

$$
∇[fh]=f\,∇\,h+h\,∇\,f\,\,
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y})={e}^{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y})=x{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$

$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{x})=y{e}^{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{x})={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y) & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\text{ }j=y{e}^{x}\text{ }i+{e}^{x}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)] & =x{e}^{y}(y{e}^{x}\text{ }i+{e}^{x}\text{ }j)+y{e}^{x}({e}^{y}\text{ }i+x{e}^{y}\text{ }j) \\  & =xy{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+x{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j+y{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+xy{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j \\  & =(x+1)y{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+x(1+y){e}^{x+y}\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+4yz-2{z}^{2}-2{y}^{2}x) \\  & =2x-2{y}^{2} \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+4yz-2{z}^{2}-2{y}^{2}x) \\  & =4z-4yx \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+4yz-2{z}^{2}-2{y}^{2}x) \\  & =4y-4z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇h(x,y,z)=2(x-{y}^{2})\,i+4(z-yx)\,j+4(y-z)\,k.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x-{y}^{2})\,i+4(z-yx)\,j+4(y-z)\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-{y}^{2} &=0, \\ z-yx &=0, \\ y-z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The first equation gives $x={y}^{2}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain $z={y}^{3}.$ Substituting $z={y}^{3}$ into the third equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}^{3} & =0 \\ y(1-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ y & =0,\,\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y=-1,$ we get $x=(-1)^{2}=1$ and $z=(-1)^{3}=-1.$

- For $y=0,$ we obtain $x={0}^{2}=0$ and $z={0}^{3}=0.$

- For $y=1,$ gives $x={1}^{2}=1$ and $z={1}^{3}=1.$

Finally, $∇h(x,y,z)=0$ at three points: $(1,-1,-1),$ $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,1,1).$

Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $$
\displaystyle T(\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix})=\begin{bmatrix}u\operatorname{ln}⁡v \\ {u}^{2}{v}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Given a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, we have $x=u\operatorname{ln}⁡v$ and $y={u}^{2}{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\frac{u}{v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u{v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2{u}^{2}v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡v & \frac{u}{v} \\ 2u{v}^{2} & 2{u}^{2}v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡v\cdot 2{u}^{2}v-\frac{u}{v}\cdot 2u{v}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}v(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-1).\end{aligned}
$$
Given the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-y)$ find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(0,\pi ).$

The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(0,\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-y))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-y))\,j \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}-y)\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}-y)\,j \\ ∇f(0,\pi ) & =2(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡({0}^{2}-\pi )\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡({0}^{2}-\pi )\,j \\  & =0\,i+j \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(0,\pi )\cdot ⟨x-0,\,y-\pi ⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨0,1⟩\cdot ⟨x,\,y-\pi ⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
At which point on the curve ${x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=xy$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$

First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =xy \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy)\,j \\  & =(-2y-x)\,i-(2x-y)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i,$ we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((-2y-x)\,i-(2x-y)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ -2y-x & =0 \\ x & =-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-2y$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =xy \\ (-2y)^{2}-{y}^{2} & =(-2y)y \\ 4{y}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =-2{y}^{2} \\ 5{y}^{2} & =0 \\ y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $y=0,$ we get $x=0,$ and the corresponding point is $(0,0).$

Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
\lim_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}
$$

I. The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=2$

II. The limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{2}$ along the path $y=x+1$

III. The limit does not exist

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & =\frac{(1-1)(2-2)}{(1-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0(0)}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(1,2)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=2}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(2-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(0)}{(x-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=x+1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=x+1}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x+1-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x+1-2)^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x-1)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x-1)^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2(x-1)^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 1}\frac{\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}}{2\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 1}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
\lim_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$

Which of the following represents the streamlines of the vector field $$
\displaystyle F(x,y)=\left(\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}\right)i+\left(\frac{2x}{y-{x}^{2}}\right)j
$$ over the domain $D=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y>{x}^{2}\}.$

The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $F$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that 

$$
F(x,y)=\left(\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}\right)i+\left(\frac{2x}{y-{x}^{2}}\right)j
$$

 is a vector field with simply connected domain $D,$ where $P(x,y)=\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}$ and $Q(x,y)=\frac{2x}{y-{x}^{2}}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{(y-{x}^{2})^{2}},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-\frac{2x}{(y-{x}^{2})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{2x}{(y-{x}^{2})^{2}}+\left(-\frac{2x}{(y-{x}^{2})^{2}}\right)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=-\frac{2x}{y-{x}^{2}}.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(y-{x}^{2})+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(y-{x}^{2})+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(y-{x}^{2}).
$$

Finally, we find the level curves of the stream function $ψ(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(y-{x}^{2})$ given by the equations $ψ(x,y)=c.$

Notice that the range of $ψ(x,y)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ So, we will consider level curves for any value of $c.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(y-{x}^{2}) & =c \\ y-{x}^{2} & ={e}^{c} \\ y & ={x}^{2}+{e}^{c}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above gives us a family of parabolas with the vertex at $(0,{e}^{c}).$ Therefore, the correct graph (along with the vector field $F$) is as follows:

![](images/ed/edc12146ffad4dc46ed6d57b3dfdc9a08ca92fb601ef5e08ed9ccef3a1c1da4c.png)

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$

Given a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=uv$ and $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{u}{v}\right).$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-\frac{1}{v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}v & u \\ \frac{1}{u} & -\frac{1}{v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =v\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{v}\right)-u\cdot \frac{1}{u} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,3)}=-2.
$$

Computing the partial derivatives of the function $ψ(x,y),$ we have

$$

Therefore, the vector field with the stream function $ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}{e}^{1-y}$ is

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field I doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\ne 0.
$$

- Vector field II has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+(-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0.
$$

- Vector field III doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2{e}^{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=1+2{e}^{y}\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field I doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2x+(-x)\ne 0.
$$

- Vector field II has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x-2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2y-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=(2x-2y)+(2y-2x)=0.

$$

The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $F$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that 

$$
F(x,y)=(x-1)i-y\,j
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$

$$

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}=x-1,\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=y.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)=xy-y+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)=xy+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f(x)=0$ or $g(y)=-y,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)=xy-y.
$$

Finally, we find the level curves of the stream function $ψ(x,y)=xy-y$ given by the equations $ψ(x,y)=c.$

Notice that the range of $ψ(x,y)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ So, we will consider level curves for any value of $c.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =c \\ xy-y & =c \\ y(x-1) & =c \\ y & =\frac{c}{x-1}\end{aligned}

Find the volume bounded by the region $R,$ given by

Recall that the volume of $R$ can be found as 

$$

$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required volume, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

The inequalities that define the region $R,$

$$
0\le y-{e}^{x}\le 1,\,1\le y\le 2,\,0\le z{e}^{-x}\le 1,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=y-{e}^{x},\,v=y,\,w=z{e}^{-x}.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required volume, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,1\le v\le 2,\,0\le w\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-{e}^{x} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -z{e}^{-x} & 0 & {e}^{-x}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-1)^{2+2}\begin{vmatrix}-{e}^{x} & 0 \\ -z{e}^{-x} & {e}^{-x}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}dV & ={∭}_{Δ}1\cdot |-1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}dw\,dv\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}du\cdot {\int }_{1}^{2}dv\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}dw \\  & =[u]_{u=0}^{u=1}\cdot [v]_{v=1}^{v=2}\cdot [w]_{w=0}^{w=1} \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (2-1)\cdot (1-0) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

At which points on the curve ${y}^{2}-xy=x+1$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$

First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-xy & =x+1 \\ {y}^{2}-xy-x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-xy-x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-xy-x)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-xy-x)j \\  & =(2y-x)\,i+(y+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((2y-x)\,i+(y+1)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2y-x & =0 \\ x & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=2y$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-(2y)y-(2y) & =1 \\ {y}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-2y-1 & =0 \\ -{y}^{2}-2y-1 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}+2y+1 & =0 \\ (y+1)^{2} & =0 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $y=-1$, we get $x=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,-1).$

Which of the following vector fields have a stream function?

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field I has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-6xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =6xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=(-6xy)+6xy=0
$$

- Vector field II doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =16{y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2+16{y}^{3}\ne 0.
$$

- Vector field III doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=1+(-3)\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v),$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨-2x,\,-2y,\,-z⟩,\,r(u,v)=⟨{u}^{3},\,{v}^{3},\,uv⟩,\,(u,v)\in D⊂{R}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-3{v}^{3},\,-3{u}^{3},\,9{u}^{2}{v}^{2}⟩.$*

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Notice we are told that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-3{v}^{3},\,-3{u}^{3},\,9{u}^{2}{v}^{2}⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨-2x,\,-2y,\,-z⟩{|}_{x={u}^{3}\,y={v}^{3}\,z=uv} \\  & =⟨-2{u}^{3},\,-2{v}^{3},\,-uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨-2{u}^{3},\,-2{v}^{3},\,-uv⟩\cdot ⟨-3{v}^{3},\,-3{u}^{3},\,9{u}^{2}{v}^{2}⟩ \\  & =(-2{u}^{3})\cdot (-3{v}^{3})+(-2{v}^{3})\cdot (-3{u}^{3})+(-uv)\cdot 9{u}^{2}{v}^{2} \\  & =6{u}^{3}{v}^{3}+6{u}^{3}{v}^{3}-9{u}^{3}{v}^{3} \\  & =3{u}^{3}{v}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,3{u}^{3}{v}^{3}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(0,0),$ $(2,-2),$ $(3,-1),$ and $(1,1).$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$

$$

suggests that we use the change of variables

First, we have to find $a+b$. The given directions are perpendicular, so the triangle law of addition gives a right triangle.

To find the unit vector corresponding to $a+b$, we have to divide by the magnitude:

$$
u=\frac{a+b}{|a+b|}
$$

To find the magnitude, we can use the Pythagorean theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}|a+b|^2&=|a|^2+|b|^2\\
&=7^2+24^2\\
&=49+576\\
&=625\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the magnitude is

$$
|a+b|=\sqrt{625}=25
$$

and the corresponding unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}u&=\frac{a+b}{|a+b|}\\
&=\frac{1}{25}(a+b)\end{aligned}
$$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}-1}=\frac{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+1}-1}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}-1} & =\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}+1)}{(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}-1)(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}+1)} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}+1)}{(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})^{2}-{1}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}+1)}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (0,0)}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (0,0)}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}+1) & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+1}+1 \\  & =\sqrt{1}+1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $2.$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (1,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & =\frac{{0}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(1,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $x\to (1,0)$ along the path $y=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (1,0)\,\,\,y=0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & =\lim_{x\to 1}\frac{{0}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-1} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (1,0)$ along the path $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (1,0)\,\,\,x=1}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & =\lim_{y\to 0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} \\  & =\lim_{y\to 0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{y\to 0}1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
\lim_{x\to (1,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1}=\text{DNE}
$$
Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=4-4z$ at the point $(0,2,2).$

First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =4-4z \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z & =4\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=4.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,2,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,2,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z)k \\  & =2x\,i-2y\,j+4\,k \\ ∇f(0,2,2) & =2(0)\,i-2(2)\text{ }j+4\,k \\  & =-4\,j+4\,k \\  & =⟨0,-4,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(0,2,2)$ and passes through the point $(0,2,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨0,2,2⟩+t\,∇f(0,2,2)=⟨0,2,2⟩+t\,⟨0,-4,4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}u+\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ v \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡u+w\end{bmatrix}.
$$

For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+\operatorname{cos}⁡w,\,y(u,v,w)=v,\,z(u,v,w)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0, & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-1)^{2+2}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\operatorname{sin}⁡w.\end{aligned}
$$
Find parametric equations for the normal line to the surface $\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=1$ at the point $(0,0,\sqrt{e}).$

Let's set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}).$ Then,  our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=1.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,0,\sqrt{e})$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,0,\sqrt{e}).$  

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,0,\sqrt{e}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))k \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\text{ }i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\text{ }j+\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,0,\sqrt{e}) & =\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(\sqrt{e})^{2}}\text{ }i+\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(\sqrt{e})^{2}}\text{ }j+\frac{2\sqrt{e}}{(0)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(\sqrt{e})^{2}}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{e}}{e}k\end{aligned}
$$

The parametric equations for the normal line to $f(x,y,z)$ at a point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ are given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={x}_{0}+{f}_{x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})t, \\ y & ={y}_{0}+{f}_{y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})t, \\ z & ={z}_{0}+{f}_{z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametic equations  for the normal line to our surface that  passes through the point $(0,0,\sqrt{e})$ can be written as 
 

$$
x=0,\,y=0,\,z=\sqrt{e}+\frac{2t\sqrt{e}}{e}
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$

$$

You may assume that $\theta $ is a fixed constant.

For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+v\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +w\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,y(u,v,w)=3v,\,z(u,v,w)=u\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0, & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3(-1)^{2+2}\begin{vmatrix}1 & \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3(1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

$∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,k \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+z\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz))\text{ }j+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})\,i+(-(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})+0\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0))\,j+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0)\,k \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k\end{aligned}

Therefore, $-\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$

Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-1,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}2 u v^{3}\\3 u^{2} + v^{2}\end{bmatrix}?
$$

Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))\approx\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\cdot\underbrace{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{\delta A}
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}\\& =\begin{vmatrix}2 v^{3}&6 u v^{2}\\6 u&2 v\end{vmatrix}\\& =(2 v^{3})\cdot (2 v)-(6 u v^{2})\cdot (6 u)\\& =- 36 u^{2} v^{2} + 4 v^{4}\\& =- 4 v^{2} \left(3 u - v\right) \left(3 u + v\right)\\\left.\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(-1,2)} & =\left(- 4 v^{2} \left(3 u - v\right) \left(3 u + v\right)\right)\big|_{u=-1,v=2}\\& =- 4 (2)^{2} \left(3 (-1) - (2)\right) \left(3 (-1) + (2)\right)\\& =-80\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & \approx|-80|\cdot\delta A\\ & =80\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}2 \left(2 u + v\right)^{2}\\\left(u - v\right)^{3}\end{bmatrix}?
$$

Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))\approx\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\cdot\underbrace{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{\delta A}
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}\\& =\begin{vmatrix}8 \left(2 u + v\right)&4 \left(2 u + v\right)\\3 \left(u - v\right)^{2}&- 3 \left(u - v\right)^{2}\end{vmatrix}\\& =(8 \left(2 u + v\right))\cdot (- 3 \left(u - v\right)^{2})-(4 \left(2 u + v\right))\cdot (3 \left(u - v\right)^{2})\\& =- 72 u^{3} + 108 u^{2} v - 36 v^{3}\\& =- 36 \left(u - v\right)^{2} \left(2 u + v\right)\\\left.\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(1,-1)} & =\left(- 36 \left(u - v\right)^{2} \left(2 u + v\right)\right)\big|_{u=1,v=-1}\\& =- 36 \left(- (-1) + (1)\right)^{2} \left((-1) + 2 (1)\right)\\& =-144\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & \approx|-144|\cdot\delta A\\ & =144\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$
