Evaluate the line integral
$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}2 x y^{6}\,\text{d}s,
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\frac{1}{y}$ from $(1,1)$ to $(\frac{1}{2},2),$ as shown above.

Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{1}{t}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{1}{t},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le 2
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 2$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =- \frac{1}{t^{2}}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\left(- \frac{1}{t^{2}}\right)^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{t^{4}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{t^{4}}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=2 x y^{6},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2 \left(\frac{1}{t}\right) t^{6} \\  & =2 t^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2 x y^{6}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\left(2 t^{5}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{t^{4}}}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2 t^{3} \sqrt{t^{4} + 1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=t^{4} + 1,$ $\text{d}u=4 t^{3}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}2 t^{3} \sqrt{t^{4} + 1}\,\text{d}t & =2{\int }_{2}^{17}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{17}\frac{\sqrt{u}}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{2}^{17} \\  & =\left[\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_{2}^{17} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{\left(17\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{\left(2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{17 \sqrt{17}}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =- \frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} + \frac{17 \sqrt{17}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the line integral
$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}2 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\text{d}s,
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=e^{\frac{y}{2}}$ from $(1,0)$ to $(\sqrt{2},\ln{\left(2 \right)}).$

Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=e^{\frac{t}{2}}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨e^{\frac{t}{2}},\,t⟩,\,0\le t\le \ln{\left(2 \right)}
$$

Note that the domain $0\le t\le \ln{\left(2 \right)}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(e^{\frac{t}{2}})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2}\right)^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{e^{t}}{4}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{e^{t}}{4} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=2 x^{6} e^{- 2 y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2 \left(e^{\frac{t}{2}}\right)^{6} e^{- 2 t} \\  & =2 e^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\left(2 e^{t}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{\frac{e^{t}}{4} + 1}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\sqrt{e^{t} + 4} e^{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=e^{t} + 4,$ $\text{d}u=e^{t}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\sqrt{e^{t} + 4} e^{t}\,\text{d}t & =1{\int }_{5}^{6}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(1\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{5}^{6}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[1\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{5}^{6} \\  & =\left[\frac{2 u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_{5}^{6} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{2 \left(6\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{2 \left(5\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(4 \sqrt{6}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{10 \sqrt{5}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =- \frac{10 \sqrt{5}}{3} + 4 \sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the line integral
$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\frac{6 x}{y}\,\text{d}s,
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $y^2=6x$ from $(\frac{7}{6},\sqrt{7})$ to $(\frac{8}{3},4).$

Notice that the given curve can be expressed in the form $x=x(y),$ as follows:

$$
y^2=6x\,⟹\,x=\frac{y^{2}}{6}.
$$

Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{t^{2}}{6}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{t^{2}}{6},\,t⟩,\,\sqrt{7}\le t\le 4
$$

Note that the domain $\sqrt{7}\le t\le 4$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{t^{2}}{6}\right)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{t}{3}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{t}{3}\right)^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{9}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{9} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{6 x}{y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{6 \left(\frac{t^{2}}{6}\right)}{t} \\  & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{6 x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\sqrt{7}}^{4}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{7}}^{4}\left(t\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{9} + 1}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{7}}^{4}\frac{t \sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=t^{2} + 9,$ $\text{d}u=2 t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\sqrt{7}}^{4}\frac{t \sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{16}^{25}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{16}^{25}\frac{\sqrt{u}}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{16}^{25} \\  & =\left[\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9}\right]_{16}^{25} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{\left(25\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{\left(16\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{125}{9}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{64}{9}\right)\right) \\  & =\frac{61}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the line integral
$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}2 y\,\text{d}s,
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=2 y + 1$ from $(5,2)$ to $(7,3).$

Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=2 t + 1.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨2 t + 1,\,t⟩,\,2\le t\le 3
$$

Note that the domain $2\le t\le 3$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t + 1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2)^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=2 y,$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2 t \\  & =2 t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2 y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{2}^{3}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}\left(2 t\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{5}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}2 \sqrt{5} t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}2 \sqrt{5} t\,\text{d}t & =\left[\sqrt{5} t^{2}\right]_{2}^{3} \\  & =2 \sqrt{5}\left(\frac{3^2}{2}-\frac{2^2}{2}\right) \\  & =2 \sqrt{5}\left(\frac{9}{2}-2\right) \\  & =5 \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}

Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
\iint_D 3 y^{2} \left(x + 2 y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(4,0)$, $(5,0)$, $(-3,4)$ and $(-4,4)$.

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=3 y^{2} \left(x + 2 y\right)
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x + 2 y,\qquad v=y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
T^{-1}:(x,y)\mapsto (u(x,y),v(x,y)).
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T^{-1}(4,0)&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(2\right)\cdot \left(0\right)+\left(0\right),\left(0\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(0\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(4,0) \\ T^{-1}(5,0)&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(5\right)+\left(2\right)\cdot \left(0\right)+\left(0\right),\left(0\right)\cdot \left(5\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(0\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(5,0) \\ T^{-1}(-3,4)&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(-3\right)+\left(2\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(0\right),\left(0\right)\cdot \left(-3\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(5,4) \\ T^{-1}(-4,4)&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(-4\right)+\left(2\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(0\right),\left(0\right)\cdot \left(-4\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(4,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):4\le u\le 5,\ 0\le v\le 4\}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\partial u/\partial x&\partial u/\partial y\\\partial v/\partial x&\partial v/\partial y\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=1
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

Solving these affine equations also gives

$$
x=u - 2 v,\qquad y=v.
$$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

$$

$$

Consider the plane curve ${x}^{3}{y}^{2}=2x+y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,1).$

First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}{y}^{2} & =2x+y \\ {x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)j \\  & =(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-2)\,i+(2{x}^{3}y-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =(3(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}-2)\,i+(2(-1)^{3}(1)-1)\,j \\  & =\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,1)=⟨1,-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{1} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x+1) & =y-1 \\ -3x-3 & =y-1 \\ 3x+y+2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$∇f(1,1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,1,1) & =\frac{1}{1}\,i+\frac{1}{1}\,j+\frac{1}{1}\,k \\  & =i+j+k\end{aligned}

Consider the part of parabola and constant vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be the path where the part of parabola is traversed from $A$ to $B.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0
$$

II. $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$

III. $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0
$$

Remember that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.
$$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.
$$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statements I is false, while statement II is true. As the particle moves from $A$ to $B,$ the force $F$ works with the particle for $y<0,$ while $F$  works against the particle for $y>0.$ 

![](images/53/537aca6190fc2f3e06e85c0781a8bb461559ef0a7515ee29aca505f9d615f820.png)

 

By symmetry, the contribution to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ for $y<0$ is canceled out by the contribution for $y>0.$ So,

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/49/4939f9a22400a7a56eaeacb77d520e522f50aa8378ca1014a19810122e12da51.png)

 

So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

Consider the vector field $F=-0.5x\,i-0.5y\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $8$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across all four sides of the square.*

If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/ab/abe90a592e098a4656577f3a2303669dccc126baff738397836c8f96c26b5389.png)

First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-0.5x\,i-0.5y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-0.5{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=4\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-4,4].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-0.5{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-0.5{\int }_{-4}^{4}4\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{-4}^{4}\text{d}t \\  & =-2(4-(-4)) \\  & =(-2)\cdot 8 \\  & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides ${C}_{2},{C}_{3},$ and ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=4\cdot (-16)=-64.
$$

Consider the vector field $F=-3\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/3b/3bd953b7fb02b90a55a29bea6f58ff9bd8bab77d62b1df1c547ca899656d37a3.png)

Now, since the vector field $F=-3\,j$ is parallel to ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{3},$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s.
$$

Now, since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through ${C}_{2}$ will cancel with the net outflow through ${C}_{4}.$ That is

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s=-{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s\,⟹\,{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,e)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-1,e)=f_y(-1,e)i-f_x(-1,e)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(4 x^{2} + x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(4 x^{2} + x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ &=(x - \frac{3 x}{y})\,i-(8 x + y - 3 \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ t(-1,e)&=(\left(-1\right) - \frac{3 \left(-1\right)}{\left(e\right)})\,i-(8 \left(-1\right) + \left(e\right) - 3 \ln{\left(\left(e\right) \right)})\,j \\ &=(-1 + \frac{3}{e})\,i-(-11 + e)\,j \\ &=-\left(1 - \frac{3}{e}\right)\, i+\left(11 - e\right)\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-\left(1 - \frac{3}{e}\right)\, i+\left(11 - e\right)\, j.$
Consider the plane curve $- 3 x^{2} + x y + 4 y=-6.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(-1,-1).$

First, if we set $f(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} + x y + 4 y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-6.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,-1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-1,-1)=f_y(-1,-1)i-f_x(-1,-1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- 3 x^{2} + x y + 4 y)\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- 3 x^{2} + x y + 4 y)\,j \\ &=(x + 4)\,i-(- 6 x + y)\,j \\ t(-1,-1)&=(\left(-1\right) + 4)\,i-(- 6 \left(-1\right) + \left(-1\right))\,j \\ &=(3)\,i-(5)\,j \\ &=3\, i-5\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $3\, i-5\, j.$
Consider the plane curve $- 3 x^{2} - x y - y=-1.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,-1).$

First, if we set $f(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} - x y - y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,-1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,-1)=f_y(1,-1)i-f_x(1,-1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- 3 x^{2} - x y - y)\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- 3 x^{2} - x y - y)\,j \\ &=(- x - 1)\,i-(- 6 x - y)\,j \\ t(1,-1)&=(- \left(1\right) - 1)\,i-(- 6 \left(1\right) - \left(-1\right))\,j \\ &=(-2)\,i-(-5)\,j \\ &=-2\, i+5\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-2\, i+5\, j.$

Consider the vector field $F=3\,i$ and a square $C$ with side length $10$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/a2/a2964076c4126d6277625260c45479d1a4fb2028f7e75223a0f5942b15f5a2d2.png)

Now, since the vector field $F=3\,i$ is parallel to ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{4},$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s.
$$

Now, since the vector field is uniform, the net outflow through ${C}_{1}$ will cancel with the net inflow through ${C}_{3}.$ That is

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=-{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s\,⟹\,{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

Use the change of variables 

$$
u=2 x + y,\quad v=y + 2 z,\quad w=3 z
$$

to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\iiint_R \left(\left(2 x + y\right) \left(y + 2 z\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}V,
$$

 
where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z):0\le 2 x + y\le 2,\quad 0\le y + 2 z\le 2,\quad 0\le z\le 2\}.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=2 x + y,\quad v=y + 2 z,\quad w=3 z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v,w):0\le u\le 2,\quad 0\le v\le 2,\quad 0\le w\le 6\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(3\right)(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(3\right)\left(\left(2\right)\cdot \left(1\right)-\left(1\right)\cdot \left(0\right)\right) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=2x+y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(-1,4)$ to $(- \frac{5}{2},2)?$

We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,4)$ to $(- \frac{5}{2},2).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+4\,j$ and $b=-\frac{5}{2}\,i+2\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-i+4\,j)+t[(-\frac{5}{2}\,i+2\,j)-(-i+4\,j)] \\  & =(-i+4\,j)+t(-\frac{3}{2}\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(-\frac{3}{2}t-1)\,i+(4-2t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-\frac{3}{2}t-1$ and $y=4-2t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{3}{2}t-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-2t)j \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\,i-2\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\left(- \frac{3}{2}\right)^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(-\frac{3}{2}t-1)+(4-2t) \\  & =-5t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-5t+2)\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-5t+2)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$

$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))$, given that

$$

$$

For a transformation

$$
T:(u,v,w)\to(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T$ is $\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}$.

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}$, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$.

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=-8 & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=0 & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}=0 \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}=0 & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=1 & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z}=0 \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=0 & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y}=0 & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}-8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=-8\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=-8\left(1\cdot 1-0\right) \\ &=-8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=- \frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2\left(y\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =2\left(x\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $2, 1, 1$ multiplies the determinant by $2$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2\left(y\right) & 2\left(x\right) & 0 \\ 0 & z & y \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\left(y\begin{vmatrix}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{vmatrix}-x\begin{vmatrix}0 & y \\ z & x\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =2\left(y(xz-0)-x(0-yz)\right)\\  & =2\left(xyz+xyz\right)\\  & =4 x y z.\end{aligned}

$$

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & v \\ 0 & 2v & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & v \\ 2v & u\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & v \\ 0 & u\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-2{v}^{2},\,-u,\,2v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x,\,y,\,xz⟩{|}_{x=u\,y={v}^{2}\,z=uv} \\  & =⟨u,\,{v}^{2},\,{u}^{2}v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u,\,{v}^{2},\,{u}^{2}v⟩\cdot ⟨-2{v}^{2},\,-u,\,2v⟩ \\  & =u\cdot (-2{v}^{2})+{v}^{2}\cdot (-u)+{u}^{2}v\cdot 2v \\  & =-2u{v}^{2}-u{v}^{2}+2{u}^{2}{v}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}{v}^{2}-3u{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\cdot {u}^{2}{v}^{2}+(-3)\cdot u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=2-3=-1.
$$

The area of the required region is given by

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=\frac{2}{x y},\,v=4 x^{3} y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=\frac{2}{x y}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{x} & ⟹\, & \frac{2}{x y}=2 & ⟹\, & u=2 \\  & y=\frac{2}{5 x} & ⟹\, & \frac{2}{x y}=5 & ⟹\, & u=5\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=4 x^{3} y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{4 x^{3}} & ⟹\, & 4 x^{3} y=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=\frac{7}{4 x^{3}} & ⟹\, & 4 x^{3} y=7 & ⟹\, & v=7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 5,\,1\le v\le 7\}
$$

![](images/d3/d3dd7067bbcb0a6e3c901d12a2795500e192594a14e7f1373dd325e4fd270363.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}- \frac{2}{x^{2} y} & - \frac{2}{x y^{2}} \\ 12 x^{2} y & 4 x^{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{16 x}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{y}{16 x}=\frac{x^{2} y^{2}}{16 x^{3} y}=\frac{1}{u^{2} v}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{u^{2} v}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\int_{2}^{5}\int_{1}^{7}\frac{1}{u^{2} v}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\  & =\int_{2}^{5}\frac{1}{u^{2}}\,\mathrm d u\int_{1}^{7}\frac{1}{v}\,\mathrm d v \\  & =(- \frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{2})\cdot (\ln 7-\ln 1) \\  & =\frac{3 \ln{\left(7 \right)}}{10}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

Find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse defined by

$$
\frac{x}{8}=\cos\theta,\quad \frac{y}{2}=\sin\theta,\quad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
$$

To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{8} & =\cos\theta \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(8)^{2}} & =\cos^2\theta \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{64} & =\cos^2\theta.\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{2} & =\sin\theta \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{(2)^{2}} & =\sin^2\theta \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =\sin^2\theta.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1,$ we get

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{64}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}=\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1.
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{64}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}=1.
$$

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(0,1)$ and $(2,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(0+t(2-0)),\,(1+t(3-1))⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,1+2t⟩,\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9\left({y}^{2}-2x\right)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9\left((1+2t)^{2}-2(2t)\right)\\  & =9\left(1+4t+4{t}^{2}-4t\right)\\  & =9\left(4{t}^{2}+1\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =9\left({\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t\right)\\  & =9\left(2{\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t\right)\\  & =9\left(2{[\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+t]}_{0}^{1}\right)\\  & =9\left(2(\frac{4}{3}+1)-2(0)\right)\\  & =9\left(\frac{14}{3}\right)\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}t,\,\operatorname{sin}t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}t)=-3\operatorname{sin}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=7\left(x{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}\right)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =7\left((3\operatorname{cos}t){e}^{1-\operatorname{sin}^{2}t}\right)\\  & =7\left(3\operatorname{cos}t{e}^{\operatorname{cos}^{2}t}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =7\left({\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}t{e}^{\operatorname{cos}^{2}t})\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}t)\cdot \text{d}t\right)\\  & =7\left(-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t{e}^{\operatorname{cos}^{2}t}\,\text{d}t\right)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$

$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}t)=2\operatorname{cos}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=7\left({x}^{2}y\right)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =7\left((\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}(2\operatorname{sin}t)\right)\\  & =7\left(2\operatorname{sin}t{cos}^{2}t\right)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$

$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$

$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\left(x + y\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- z\right)\,k \\ & =\left(4\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(4 - 4 t^{2}\right)\,i+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(4 t^{2}\right)\,j+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k \\ & =\left(- 8 t\right)\,i+\left(8 t\right)\,j+\left(\pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Remember that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.
$$

- If the force works *against* the motion  of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.
$$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0
$$ is false, while statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$ is true. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion.

So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

- Statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0
$$ is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ the force is still perpendicular to the motion.

![](images/50/508e0ac5f67d7b119ad689ccaede8894268eefe31d9b00f148ddd6bf851de6b4.png)

So, $$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i-z\,j+y\,k \\  & =2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =0\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =2\cdot 0+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\pi \,\text{d}t \\  & =\pi [t]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\pi (2-0) \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$

$$

Given a transformation 

$$

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}$, is given by

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=4 u \cos{\left(v \right)}$ and $y(u,v)=2 u \sin{\left(v \right)}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&=4 \cos{\left(v \right)}&\quad \frac{\partial x}{\partial v}&=- 4 u \sin{\left(v \right)}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&=2 \sin{\left(v \right)}&\quad \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}&=2 u \cos{\left(v \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\begin{vmatrix}4 \cos{\left(v \right)}&- 4 u \sin{\left(v \right)}\\2 \sin{\left(v \right)}&2 u \cos{\left(v \right)}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\left(4 \cos{\left(v \right)}\right)\cdot\left(2 u \cos{\left(v \right)}\right)\\&\quad{}-\left(- 4 u \sin{\left(v \right)}\right)\cdot\left(2 \sin{\left(v \right)}\right)\\&=8 u\left(\cos^2 v+\sin^2 v\right)\\&=8 u.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F=4x\,\mathbf i+y\,\mathbf j$ and a square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*

If $\mathbf F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds,
$$

where $\mathbf n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds+\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds\\
&\quad+\int_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_3\,\mathrm ds+\int_{C_4}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_4\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/83/83bf612af65f14848f10293bea459e926cd8246c2c48ea223709becd7acc1b1b.png)

We compute this integral in two stages.

- First, consider the side $C_1.$ We have that $\mathbf n_1=\mathbf i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_1}(4x\,\mathbf i+y\,\mathbf j)\cdot\mathbf i\,\mathrm ds\\
&=4\int_{C_1}x\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_1,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t)=2\mathbf i+t\,\mathbf j,\quad \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf j,\quad t\in[-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
4\int_{C_1}x\,\mathrm ds
&=4\int_{-2}^{2}2\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt\\
&=(8)\int_{-2}^{2}\mathrm dt\\
&=(8)\cdot 4\\
&=32.
\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_3$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds=\int_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_3\,\mathrm ds=32.
$$

- Next, consider the side $C_2.$ We have that $\mathbf n_2=\mathbf j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_2}(4x\,\mathbf i+y\,\mathbf j)\cdot\mathbf j\,\mathrm ds\\
&=\int_{C_2}y\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_2,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+2\mathbf j,\quad \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf i,\quad t\in[-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{C_2}y\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{-2}^{2}2\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt\\
&=(2)\int_{-2}^{2}\mathrm dt\\
&=(2)\cdot 4\\
&=8.
\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_4$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds=\int_{C_4}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_4\,\mathrm ds=8.
$$

Finally, then

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds=2\cdot(32)+2\cdot(8)=80.
$$

What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)$ if $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ and $h(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)?$

The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=f∇h+h∇f.
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)=yz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz)=xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)=xy\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\text{ }k=yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $h(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)] & =f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)+h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z) \\  & =xyz(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =\frac{xyz}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{xyz}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{xyz}{z}\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Hence, 

$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $g(x,y):$

$$

$$

$$

Which of the following vector fields have a stream function?

I. $F(x,y)=3{x}^{2}\,i-3{y}^{2}\,j$

II. $F(x,y)=2x\,i-2y\,j$

III. $F(x,y)=x{y}^{3}\,i+y\,j$

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field I doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=6x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-6y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=6x+(-6y)\ne 0.
$$

- Vector field II does have a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2+(-2)=0.
$$

- Vector field III doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3x{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=3x{y}^{2}+1\ne 0.

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{DF}\times \overset{\to }{DG} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}i-\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}j+\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix}k \\  & =(2\cdot 1-3\cdot 1)i-(0\cdot 1-0\cdot 1)j+(0\cdot 3-0\cdot 2)k \\  & =-i \\  & =⟨-1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}

\displaystyle \frac{{x}^{2}}{100}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{49}=1?
$$

Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=100$ and ${b}^{2}=49.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=100,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{100}=10.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=49,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{49}=7.$

So the semi-major axis has length $a=10,$ and the semi-minor axis has length $b=7.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2a=2\cdot 10=20,$ and the minor axis has length $2b=2\cdot 7=14.$

What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation 
$$

$$

$$

$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=33$ and ${b}^{2}=61.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=33,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{33}.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=61,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{61}.$

So the semi-major axis has length $b=\sqrt{61},$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=\sqrt{33}.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot \sqrt{61}=2\sqrt{61},$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot \sqrt{33}=2\sqrt{33}.$

Consider the semicircle and constant vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be the path where the semicircle is traversed from $A$ to $B.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0
$$

II. $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$

III. $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$

Remember that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.
$$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.
$$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statements I is false, while statement II is true. As the particle moves from $A$ to $B,$ the force $F$ works against the particle for $y<0,$ while $F$ works with the particle for $y>0.$ 

![](images/30/306fdb7f7a6054d214940d1ca9614c35905f015f34d175561a7850781b751a93.png)

 
By symmetry, the contribution to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ for $y<0$ is canceled out by the contribution for $y>0.$ So, 

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

- Statement III is true. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/c9/c9ea0397e7ba2a2ce6aef1058c6935a3282e12df5adc3b3d564cfb87c5f76c3b.png)

 
So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨-y,\,-z,\,-xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2{u}^{2},\,-v,\,3uv⟩
$$

over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,-1\le v\le 1\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨3v,\,-12{u}^{2},\,-4u⟩.$*

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We're given that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨3v,\,-12{u}^{2},\,-4u⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨-y,\,-z,\,-xy⟩|}_{x=2{u}^{2}\,y=-v\,z=3uv} \\  & =⟨-(-v),\,-3uv,\,-(2{u}^{2})(-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨v,\,-3uv,\,2{u}^{2}v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨v,\,-3uv,\,2{u}^{2}v⟩\cdot ⟨3v,\,-12{u}^{2},\,-4u⟩ \\  & =v\cdot 3v+(-3uv)\cdot (-12{u}^{2})+2{u}^{2}v\cdot (-4u) \\  & =3{v}^{2}+36{u}^{3}v-8{u}^{3}v \\  & =3{v}^{2}+28{u}^{3}v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-y,\,-z,\,-xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{v}^{2}+28{u}^{3}v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(3{v}^{2}+28{u}^{3}v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{v}^{3}+14{u}^{3}{v}^{2}]_{v=-1}^{v=1}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1-(-1)+14{u}^{3}-14{u}^{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2\,\text{d}u \\  & =2[u]_{0}^{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=({t}^{2}-t)\,i+(2{t}^{2}-2t+1)\,j+({t}^{2}-{t}^{3})\,k$ for $t\in [0,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=xz\,j+k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y=2{t}^{2}-2t+1,\,z={t}^{2}-{t}^{3}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =xz\,j+k \\  & =({t}^{2}-t)({t}^{2}-{t}^{3})\,j+k \\  & =(-{t}^{5}+2{t}^{4}-{t}^{3})\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-2t+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-{t}^{3})\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(4t-2)\,j+(2t-3{t}^{2})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((-{t}^{5}+2{t}^{4}-{t}^{3})\,j+k)\cdot ((2t-1)\,i+(4t-2)\,j+(2t-3{t}^{2})\,k) \\  & =0\cdot (2t-1)+(-{t}^{5}+2{t}^{4}-{t}^{3})\cdot (4t-2)+1\cdot (2t-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =2t-3{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}-8{t}^{4}+10{t}^{5}-4{t}^{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t-3{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}-8{t}^{4}+10{t}^{5}-4{t}^{6})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{4}-\frac{8}{5}{t}^{5}+\frac{5}{3}{t}^{6}-\frac{4}{7}{t}^{7}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1-1+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{8}{5}+\frac{5}{3}-\frac{4}{7} \\  & =-\frac{1}{210}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Given that the determinant of 
$$
\displaystyle \begin{bmatrix}1 - 2 p & 5 & 2 p + 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 5 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$ 
is $-38,$  find the value of $p.$

Expand along the first row, using the signs $+,-,+$. Compute the three signed contributions separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{1} & =(1 - 2 p)\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1 - 2 p)((3)(2)-(0)(-2)) \\  & =(1 - 2 p)(6) \\  & =6 - 12 p\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{2} & =-(5)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(5)((1)(2)-(0)(5)) \\  & =-(5)(2) \\  & =-10\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{3} & =(2 p + 1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 5 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(2 p + 1)((1)(-2)-(3)(5)) \\  & =(2 p + 1)(-17) \\  & =- 34 p - 17\end{aligned}
$$

Add the signed contributions to obtain the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =T_1+T_2+T_3 \\  & =- 46 p - 21\end{aligned}
$$

Set the determinant equal to the given value.

$$
\begin{aligned}- 46 p - 21 & =-38 \\ - 46 p & =-17 \\ p & =\frac{17}{46}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $p=\frac{17}{46}$.
Find the possible values of the constant $k$ given that the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -4 \\ 2 k + 1 & 3 & k \\ -5 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ is singular.

Expand along the first row, using the signs $+,-,+$. Compute the three signed contributions separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{1} & =(-1)\begin{vmatrix}3 & k \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)((3)(1)-(k)(0)) \\  & =(-1)(3) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{2} & =-(1)\begin{vmatrix}2 k + 1 & k \\ -5 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(1)((2 k + 1)(1)-(k)(-5)) \\  & =-(1)(7 k + 1) \\  & =- 7 k - 1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{3} & =(-4)\begin{vmatrix}2 k + 1 & 3 \\ -5 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-4)((2 k + 1)(0)-(3)(-5)) \\  & =(-4)(15) \\  & =-60\end{aligned}
$$

Add the signed contributions to obtain the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =T_1+T_2+T_3 \\  & =- 7 k - 64\end{aligned}
$$

A singular matrix has determinant $0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}- 7 k - 64 & =0 \\ - 7 k & =64 \\ k & =- \frac{64}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $k=- \frac{64}{7}$.

Treat the other two variables as constants in each partial derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}g_x(x,y,z)&=2x+0-0=2x \\ g_y(x,y,z)&=0+3y^2-0=3y^2 \\ g_z(x,y,z)&=0+0-2z=-2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Place the partial derivatives in the $x,y,z$ order:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla g(x,y,z)&=g_x\,\mathbf i+g_y\,\mathbf j+g_z\,\mathbf k \\ &=2x\,\mathbf i+3y^2\,\mathbf j-2z\,\mathbf k.\end{aligned}
$$

Apply the chain rule while holding the other two variables constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y,z)&=\frac{y(z+1)}{2\sqrt{xy(z+1)}}=\frac{\sqrt{xy(z+1)}}{2x} \\ f_y(x,y,z)&=\frac{x(z+1)}{2\sqrt{xy(z+1)}}=\frac{\sqrt{xy(z+1)}}{2y} \\ f_z(x,y,z)&=\frac{xy}{2\sqrt{xy(z+1)}}=\frac{\sqrt{xy(z+1)}}{2(z+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

The stated domain makes all denominators nonzero. Assemble the gradient:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(x,y,z)&=f_x\,\mathbf i+f_y\,\mathbf j+f_z\,\mathbf k \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{xy(z+1)}}{2}\left(\frac{1}{x}\,\mathbf i+\frac{1}{y}\,\mathbf j+\frac{1}{z+1}\,\mathbf k\right).\end{aligned}
$$

In the $y$ partial derivative, both factors depend on $y$, so use the product rule as well as the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}h_x(x,y,z)&=ye^{xy}\cos(yz) \\ h_y(x,y,z)&=xe^{xy}\cos(yz)-ze^{xy}\sin(yz) \\ h_z(x,y,z)&=-ye^{xy}\sin(yz).\end{aligned}
$$

Assemble the gradient in coordinate order:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla h(x,y,z)&=h_x\,\mathbf i+h_y\,\mathbf j+h_z\,\mathbf k \\
&=ye^{xy}\cos(yz)\,\mathbf i \\
&\quad+e^{xy}(x\cos(yz)-z\sin(yz))\,\mathbf j \\
&\quad-ye^{xy}\sin(yz)\,\mathbf k.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the stated point, $xy=2$, $yz=\frac{\pi}{4}$, and $\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}h_x(2,1,\tfrac{\pi}{4})&=\frac{e^2\sqrt{2}}{2} \\
h_y(2,1,\tfrac{\pi}{4})&=e^2\left(2\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\pi}{4}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\
h_z(2,1,\tfrac{\pi}{4})&=-\frac{e^2\sqrt{2}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla h(2,1,\tfrac{\pi}{4})& \\
&=\frac{e^2\sqrt{2}}{2}\left(\mathbf i+\left(2-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\,\mathbf j-\mathbf k\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

For $f(x,y)=(x-2)^2+(y+1)^2$, the gradient is

$$
\nabla f(x,y)=2(x-2)\mathbf i+2(y+1)\mathbf j.
$$

Find the point $(x,y)$ where $\nabla f(x,y)=\mathbf 0$. Both components must be zero at the same point.

A vector is zero exactly when every component is zero. Thus we solve

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2(x-2) &= 0 \\ 2(y+1) &= 0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The first equation gives $x=2$ and the second gives $y=-1$. At $(2,-1)$, the gradient is $0\mathbf i+0\mathbf j$.

Therefore, the only point is $(2,-1)$.

Given $h(x,y,z)=(x-1)^2+4yz-2z^2-2(x-1)y^2$, find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $\nabla h(x,y,z)=\mathbf 0$.

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.

First, find all three partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_x &= 2(x-1)-2y^2, \\
h_y &= 4z-4(x-1)y, \\
h_z &= 4y-4z.
\end{aligned}
$$

Setting every component of the gradient equal to zero and removing nonzero constant factors gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-1-y^2 &= 0 \\ z-(x-1)y &= 0 \\ y-z &= 0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The first equation gives $x-1=y^2$, and the third gives $z=y$. Substitute both into the second:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-y^3 &= 0, \\
y(1-y)(1+y) &= 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $y=0$, $y=1$, or $y=-1$. Dividing by $y$ would lose the $y=0$ branch. Recover the remaining coordinates from $x=1+y^2$ and $z=y$:

- If $y=0$, then $x=1$ and $z=0$, giving $(1,0,0)$.
- If $y=1$, then $x=2$ and $z=1$, giving $(2,1,1)$.
- If $y=-1$, then $x=2$ and $z=-1$, giving $(2,-1,-1)$.

Each point satisfies all three component equations, and the factorization exhausts the possibilities. Therefore, the points are $(1,0,0)$, $(2,1,1)$, and $(2,-1,-1)$.
Given $g(x,y)=x^2+xy+y^2-5x-4y$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $\nabla g(x,y)=\mathbf 0$.

First, differentiate with respect to each variable, treating the other as constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_x &= 2x+y-5, \\
g_y &= x+2y-4.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\nabla g=(2x+y-5)\mathbf i+(x+2y-4)\mathbf j$. Both components must vanish:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y &= 5 \\ x+2y &= 4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, $y=5-2x$. Substituting into the second gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
x+2(5-2x) &= 4, \\
-3x+10 &= 4, \\
x &= 2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Then $y=5-2(2)=1$. Checking both components gives $2(2)+1-5=0$ and $2+2(1)-4=0$.

Therefore, the only point is $(2,1)$.

$$

$$

A square matrix is singular if and only if its determinant is zero.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\det(H) &= (-3)\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & -5\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ -1 & -5\end{vmatrix} \\

&= (-3)\cdot 1 \\
&\quad +1\cdot 6 \\

$$

Since $\det(H)=0$, $H$ is singular.

For the functions below, both gradients are supplied:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,y)&=x+y, & \nabla f(x,y)&=\mathbf i+\mathbf j,\\
g(x,y)&=x-2y, & \nabla g(x,y)&=\mathbf i-2\mathbf j.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use $\nabla(fg)=g\nabla f+f\nabla g$. Which expression gives $\nabla(fg)$? You do not need to expand the products.

In each product-rule term, multiply one function by the gradient of the other:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla(fg)&=g\nabla f+f\nabla g\\
&=(x-2y)(\mathbf i+\mathbf j)+(x+y)(\mathbf i-2\mathbf j).
\end{aligned}
$$

This is already the requested expression. If expanded, its components are $(2x-y)\mathbf i+(-x-4y)\mathbf j$.

Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y)$, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,y)&=x^2-y, & \nabla f(x,y)&=2x\mathbf i-\mathbf j,\\
g(x,y)&=xy, & \nabla g(x,y)&=y\mathbf i+x\mathbf j.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the gradient product rule, $\nabla(fg)=g\nabla f+f\nabla g$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla(fg)&=xy(2x\mathbf i-\mathbf j)+(x^2-y)(y\mathbf i+x\mathbf j)\\
&=2x^2y\mathbf i-xy\mathbf j+(x^2y-y^2)\mathbf i+(x^3-xy)\mathbf j\\
&=(3x^2y-y^2)\mathbf i+(x^3-2xy)\mathbf j.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both product-rule terms contribute to each component. Combine the coefficients of $\mathbf i$ separately from those of $\mathbf j$.

What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y)$ if

$$
f(x,y)=x^2y,\qquad g(x,y)=e^{x-y^2}?
$$

First compute the two gradients. When taking a partial derivative, hold the other variable constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x&=2xy, & f_y&=x^2,\\
g_x&=e^{x-y^2}, & g_y&=-2y e^{x-y^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $-2y$ in $g_y$ comes from differentiating the exponent $x-y^2$ with respect to $y$. Thus

$$
\nabla f=2xy\mathbf i+x^2\mathbf j,\qquad
\nabla g=e^{x-y^2}\mathbf i-2y e^{x-y^2}\mathbf j.
$$

Now apply $\nabla(fg)=g\nabla f+f\nabla g$ and collect components:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla(fg)&=e^{x-y^2}(2xy\mathbf i+x^2\mathbf j)\\
&\quad+x^2y(e^{x-y^2}\mathbf i-2y e^{x-y^2}\mathbf j)\\
&=e^{x-y^2}((2xy+x^2y)\mathbf i+(x^2-2x^2y^2)\mathbf j)\\
&=e^{x-y^2}(xy(x+2)\mathbf i+x^2(1-2y^2)\mathbf j).
\end{aligned}

Find all real values of $p$ for which the following matrix is singular.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 2 \\ - 3 p - 4 & 4 p + 7 & - 3 p - 3 \\ - 5 p - 8 & 6 p + 13 & - 5 p - 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Expand along the first row, using the signs $+,-,+$. Compute the three signed contributions separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{1} & =(1)\begin{vmatrix}4 p + 7 & - 3 p - 3 \\ 6 p + 13 & - 5 p - 9\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1)((4 p + 7)(- 5 p - 9)-(- 3 p - 3)(6 p + 13)) \\  & =(1)(- 2 p^{2} - 14 p - 24) \\  & =- 2 p^{2} - 14 p - 24\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{2} & =-(-2)\begin{vmatrix}- 3 p - 4 & - 3 p - 3 \\ - 5 p - 8 & - 5 p - 9\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(-2)((- 3 p - 4)(- 5 p - 9)-(- 3 p - 3)(- 5 p - 8)) \\  & =-(-2)(8 p + 12) \\  & =16 p + 24\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{3} & =(2)\begin{vmatrix}- 3 p - 4 & 4 p + 7 \\ - 5 p - 8 & 6 p + 13\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(2)((- 3 p - 4)(6 p + 13)-(4 p + 7)(- 5 p - 8)) \\  & =(2)(2 p^{2} + 4 p + 4) \\  & =4 p^{2} + 8 p + 8\end{aligned}
$$

Add the signed contributions to obtain the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =T_1+T_2+T_3 \\  & =2 p^{2} + 10 p + 8\end{aligned}
$$

A singular matrix has determinant $0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}2 p^{2} + 10 p + 8 & =0 \\ 2 (p + 1) (p + 4) & =0 \\ p & =-4,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $p=-4$ and $p=-1$.

Find all real values of $p$ for which the following matrix is singular.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}- p - 2 & - 2 p - 3 & p + 1 \\ 3 p + 3 & 4 p + 7 & - 3 p - 5 \\ -1 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Expand along the first row, using the signs $+,-,+$. Compute the three signed contributions separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{1} & =(- p - 2)\begin{vmatrix}4 p + 7 & - 3 p - 5 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(- p - 2)((4 p + 7)(2)-(- 3 p - 5)(-2)) \\  & =(- p - 2)(2 p + 4) \\  & =- 2 p^{2} - 8 p - 8\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{2} & =-(- 2 p - 3)\begin{vmatrix}3 p + 3 & - 3 p - 5 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(- 2 p - 3)((3 p + 3)(2)-(- 3 p - 5)(-1)) \\  & =-(- 2 p - 3)(3 p + 1) \\  & =6 p^{2} + 11 p + 3\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{3} & =(p + 1)\begin{vmatrix}3 p + 3 & 4 p + 7 \\ -1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(p + 1)((3 p + 3)(-2)-(4 p + 7)(-1)) \\  & =(p + 1)(1 - 2 p) \\  & =- 2 p^{2} - p + 1\end{aligned}
$$

Add the signed contributions to obtain the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =T_1+T_2+T_3 \\  & =2 p^{2} + 2 p - 4\end{aligned}
$$

A singular matrix has determinant $0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}2 p^{2} + 2 p - 4 & =0 \\ 2 (p - 1) (p + 2) & =0 \\ p & =-2,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $p=-2$ and $p=1$.

Find all real values of $p$ for which the following matrix is singular.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}- 2 p - 1 & p & p + 2 \\ 2 p - 1 & 1 - p & - p \\ -2 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Expand along the first row, using the signs $+,-,+$. Compute the three signed contributions separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{1} & =(- 2 p - 1)\begin{vmatrix}1 - p & - p \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(- 2 p - 1)((1 - p)(2)-(- p)(1)) \\  & =(- 2 p - 1)(2 - p) \\  & =2 p^{2} - 3 p - 2\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{2} & =-(p)\begin{vmatrix}2 p - 1 & - p \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(p)((2 p - 1)(2)-(- p)(-2)) \\  & =-(p)(2 p - 2) \\  & =- 2 p^{2} + 2 p\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{3} & =(p + 2)\begin{vmatrix}2 p - 1 & 1 - p \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(p + 2)((2 p - 1)(1)-(1 - p)(-2)) \\  & =(p + 2)(1) \\  & =p + 2\end{aligned}
$$

Add the signed contributions to obtain the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =T_1+T_2+T_3 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant is $0$ for every real value of $p$. Therefore, the matrix is singular for every real value of $p$.

Find all real values of $p$ for which the following matrix is singular.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 p & - p - 1 & 1 - p \\ -2 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 p - 5 & 4 - p & 3 - p\end{bmatrix}
$$

Expand along the first row, using the signs $+,-,+$. Compute the three signed contributions separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{1} & =(2 p)\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 4 - p & 3 - p\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(2 p)((2)(3 - p)-(1)(4 - p)) \\  & =(2 p)(2 - p) \\  & =- 2 p^{2} + 4 p\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{2} & =-(- p - 1)\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 2 p - 5 & 3 - p\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(- p - 1)((-2)(3 - p)-(1)(2 p - 5)) \\  & =-(- p - 1)(-1) \\  & =- p - 1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{3} & =(1 - p)\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 2 \\ 2 p - 5 & 4 - p\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1 - p)((-2)(4 - p)-(2)(2 p - 5)) \\  & =(1 - p)(2 - 2 p) \\  & =2 p^{2} - 4 p + 2\end{aligned}
$$

Add the signed contributions to obtain the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =T_1+T_2+T_3 \\  & =1 - p\end{aligned}
$$

A singular matrix has determinant $0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}1 - p & =0 \\ - p & =-1 \\ p & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $p=1$.
Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2-y$ that passes through the point $(1,1)$.

The gradient at the given point is normal to the level curve. First find the partial derivatives, treating the other variable as constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=2x, & f_y(x,y)&=4y-1,\\
\nabla f(x,y)&=2x\,i+(4y-1)\,j,\\
\nabla f(1,1)&=2\,i+3\,j.
\end{aligned}
$$

This gradient is nonzero. Its magnitude is

$$
\|\nabla f(1,1)\|=\sqrt{2^2+3^2}=\sqrt{13}.
$$

Divide by this magnitude to obtain a unit normal vector:

$$
\mathbf n=\frac{\nabla f(1,1)}{\|\nabla f(1,1)\|}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}(2\,i+3\,j).
$$

Its negative is also a unit normal vector. Of the displayed choices, only the vector above is both parallel to the gradient and of length one.
Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\ln(x+2y)-xy$ that passes through the point $(2,0)$.

At the point $(2,0)$, the logarithm has positive argument $2$, so the function is differentiable nearby. A nonzero gradient there is normal to the level curve.

Differentiate before substituting the coordinates. The chain rule for the logarithm and the derivatives of $-xy$ give

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=\frac{1}{x+2y}-y,\\
f_y(x,y)&=\frac{2}{x+2y}-x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla f(2,0)&=\left(\frac{1}{2}-0\right)i+\left(\frac{2}{2}-2\right)j\\
&=\frac{1}{2}i-j,\\
\|\nabla f(2,0)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2+(-1)^2}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Normalize this nonzero vector:

$$
\mathbf n=\frac{\frac{1}{2}i-j}{\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(i-2\,j).
$$

Its negative is also a unit normal vector. Omitting the derivatives of $-xy$ gives a different direction; keeping the gradient without normalization gives the wrong length.
Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=e^{x-y}\sin(x+y)$ that passes through the point $\left(\frac{\pi}{6},0\right)$.

The function is differentiable everywhere. To find a normal vector to its level curve, compute the gradient at the specified point. Apply the product and chain rules to both partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=e^{x-y}\sin(x+y)+e^{x-y}\cos(x+y),\\
f_y(x,y)&=-e^{x-y}\sin(x+y)+e^{x-y}\cos(x+y).
\end{aligned}
$$

At $\left(\frac{\pi}{6},0\right)$, use $\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$:

$$
\nabla f\left(\frac{\pi}{6},0\right)=\frac{e^{\pi/6}}{2}\left((1+\sqrt{3})\,i+(\sqrt{3}-1)\,j\right).
$$

The common factor is positive, and this vector is nonzero. Its magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|\nabla f\left(\frac{\pi}{6},0\right)\right\|
&=\frac{e^{\pi/6}}{2}\sqrt{(1+\sqrt{3})^2+(\sqrt{3}-1)^2}\\
&=\frac{e^{\pi/6}}{2}\sqrt{(4+2\sqrt{3})+(4-2\sqrt{3})}\\
&=e^{\pi/6}\sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Divide the gradient by its magnitude. The positive exponential factor cancels:

$$
\mathbf n=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\left((1+\sqrt{3})\,i+(\sqrt{3}-1)\,j\right).
$$

Its negative is also a unit normal vector. Both product-rule terms matter: differentiating only the sine factor would incorrectly give the direction $i+j$.
Consider the plane curve $2xy=x^2+3y^2-9.$ Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at $(1,2).$

Bring the terms to one side:

$$
x^2+3y^2-2xy-9=0.
$$

Set $f(x,y)=x^2+3y^2-2xy-9.$ The curve is the level set $f(x,y)=0.$ Its gradient at $(1,2)$ supplies a normal direction:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=2x-2y, & f_y(x,y)&=6y-2x,\\
\nabla f(1,2)&=\langle 2-4,12-2\rangle\\
&=\langle -2,10\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

The line through $(1,2)$ parallel to $\langle -2,10\rangle$ has equation

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{x-1}{-2}&=\frac{y-2}{10},\\
10(x-1)&=-2(y-2),\\
5x+y-7&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the normal line is $5x+y-7=0.$ Its slope is $-5.$ In contrast, the tangent line has slope $1/5$ and equation $-x+5y-9=0.$

Consider the plane curve

$$
\frac{(x-1)^2}{4}+\frac{(y+2)^2}{9}=1.
$$

Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at $(1,1).$

Set

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{(x-1)^2}{4}+\frac{(y+2)^2}{9}.
$$

The curve is the level set $f(x,y)=1.$ Compute its gradient:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla f(x,y)&=\left\langle \frac{x-1}{2},\frac{2(y+2)}{9}\right\rangle,\\
\nabla f(1,1)&=\left\langle 0,\frac{2}{3}\right\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero and points vertically. The normal line is therefore the vertical line through $(1,1):$

$$
x=1.
$$

We can also use the relation $b(x-x_0)=a(y-y_0)$ for a line parallel to $\langle a,b\rangle:$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2}{3}(x-1)&=0(y-1),\\
x&=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

This form handles the zero first component without division by zero. The line $y=1$ is the horizontal tangent, whereas $x=0$ has the normal direction but misses the given point.

Consider the plane curve $x^2+2y^2=3.$ Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at $(1,1).$

Use $f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2.$ The vector $\nabla f(1,1)$ gives the direction of the normal line. For a direction vector $\langle a,b\rangle,$ a line through $(x_0,y_0)$ satisfies $b(x-x_0)=a(y-y_0).$

The curve is the level curve $f(x,y)=3.$ Compute the partial derivatives, then evaluate the gradient at the given point:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=2x, & f_y(x,y)&=4y,\\
\nabla f(1,1)&=\langle 2,4\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since this gradient is nonzero, it is a direction vector for the normal line. Using $a=2,$ $b=4,$ and $(x_0,y_0)=(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
4(x-1)&=2(y-1),\\
2(x-1)&=y-1,\\
2x-y-1&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the normal line is $2x-y-1=0.$ It passes through $(1,1)$ and has slope $2,$ the slope of the vector $\langle 2,4\rangle.$ The equation $x+2y-3=0$ instead describes the tangent line.

Let

$$
f(x,y,z)=(x^2+y^2+z^2-1)^2.
$$

Find a nonzero normal vector at $P=(1,0,0)$ to the level surface of $f$ that passes through $P$.

First determine which level surface passes through $P$. Since $f(1,0,0)=0$, its equation is

$$
(x^2+y^2+z^2-1)^2=0.
$$

A real number has square zero exactly when it is zero, so this is the sphere

$$
x^2+y^2+z^2=1.
$$

Direct differentiation of the supplied function gives

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z)=4(x^2+y^2+z^2-1)(x\,\mathbf i+y\,\mathbf j+z\,\mathbf k),
$$

so $\nabla f(P)=\mathbf 0$. The zero vector has no direction and is not a normal vector. A zero gradient means that this defining function does not supply a normal through the nonzero-gradient rule; it does not mean that the surface has no normal.

Use the equivalent defining function $g(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2+z^2-1$ for the same surface. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla g(x,y,z)&=2x\,\mathbf i+2y\,\mathbf j+2z\,\mathbf k,\\
\nabla g(1,0,0)&=2\,\mathbf i\ne\mathbf 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus every nonzero multiple of $\mathbf i$ is normal here. The listed vector $-3\,\mathbf i=-\frac{3}{2}\nabla g(P)$ is a normal vector. The vectors $\mathbf j$ and $\mathbf k$ are tangent directions, and $\mathbf i+\mathbf j$ is not parallel to the normal.
For the function $f(x,y,z)=x^2+xy+z^2$, find a vector perpendicular to the level surface that passes through $P=(1,-1,2)$.

A nonzero gradient at $P$ is a normal vector to the level surface through $P$. First compute the three partial derivatives, treating the other variables as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x&=2x+y, & f_y&=x, & f_z&=2z. 
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla f(x,y,z)&=(2x+y)\,\mathbf i+x\,\mathbf j+2z\,\mathbf k,\\
\nabla f(1,-1,2)&=(2(1)-1)\,\mathbf i+1\,\mathbf j+2(2)\,\mathbf k\\
&=\mathbf i+\mathbf j+4\,\mathbf k.
\end{aligned}
$$

This vector is nonzero, so $\mathbf i+\mathbf j+4\,\mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the level surface at $P$.

at $P=(1,1,1)$.

Write the surface as a level surface by moving all terms to one side:

$$
F(x,y,z)=x^2+xy+z^2-y-2.
$$

The surface has equation $F(x,y,z)=0$. The point lies on it because $F(1,1,1)=1+1+1-1-2=0$. Compute the gradient of the whole defining function, including the term $-y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla F(x,y,z)&=(2x+y)\,\mathbf i+(x-1)\,\mathbf j+2z\,\mathbf k,\\
\nabla F(1,1,1)&=3\,\mathbf i+0\,\mathbf j+2\,\mathbf k.
\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero. Every nonzero scalar multiple of it is also normal to the surface. In particular,

$$
-2\nabla F(1,1,1)=-6\,\mathbf i-4\,\mathbf k.
$$

Therefore, $-6\,\mathbf i-4\,\mathbf k$ is the listed normal vector. Differentiating only the left side would incorrectly leave a $\mathbf j$ component.

The surface $x^2+2y^2-z=0$ contains the point $P(1,-1,3)$. For $F(x,y,z)=x^2+2y^2-z$, you are given

$$
\nabla F(1,-1,3)=\langle 2,-4,-1\rangle.
$$

Which vector equation describes the normal line to the surface at $P$? Use $t\in\mathbb R$, with $t=0$ at $P$.

A nonzero gradient of a level function is perpendicular to its level surface. Thus $\langle 2,-4,-1\rangle$ is a direction vector for the normal line.

The position vector of $P$ is $\langle 1,-1,3\rangle$. A line through $P$ with direction vector $\mathbf n$ has equation $\mathbf r=\mathbf p+t\mathbf n$, so

$$
\mathbf r=\langle 1,-1,3\rangle+t\langle 2,-4,-1\rangle,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
$$

At $t=0$ this gives $P$. The point supplies the constant vector, and the gradient supplies the direction vector; they have different roles.
Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $e^{xy}+z^2=x+1$ at the point $(1,0,1)$.

Move the variable term $x$ to the left and set

$$
F(x,y,z)=e^{xy}+z^2-x.
$$

The surface is the level surface $F=1$. Using the chain rule for $e^{xy}$ gives

$$
\nabla F(x,y,z)=\langle ye^{xy}-1,\ xe^{xy},\ 2z\rangle.
$$

At $P=(1,0,1)$, we have $e^{xy}=e^0=1$, so

$$
\nabla F(1,0,1)=\langle 0(1)-1,\ 1(1),\ 2(1)\rangle=\langle -1,1,2\rangle.
$$

The gradient is nonzero and supplies the direction of the normal line. Thus a vector equation is

$$
\mathbf r=\langle 1,0,1\rangle+t\langle -1,1,2\rangle,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
$$

Writing $x=1-t$, $y=t$, and $z=1+2t$ and eliminating $t$ gives

$$
\frac{x-1}{-1}=\frac{y-0}{1}=\frac{z-1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the required equation is

$$
1-x=y=\frac{z-1}{2}.
$$
Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $z=x^2+xy+2y^2$ at $P(1,-1,2)$. Use $t\in\mathbb R$, with $t=0$ at $P$.

Bring all variable terms to one side and define

$$
F(x,y,z)=x^2+xy+2y^2-z.
$$

The surface is the level surface $F=0$. Its gradient is

$$
\nabla F(x,y,z)=\langle 2x+y,\ x+4y,\ -1\rangle.
$$

Evaluate at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla F(1,-1,2)&=\langle 2(1)-1,\ 1+4(-1),\ -1\rangle\\
&=\langle 1,-3,-1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

This nonzero vector is normal to the surface. Using $P$ as the base point, the normal line is

$$
\mathbf r=\langle 1,-1,2\rangle+t\langle 1,-3,-1\rangle,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
$$

The constant vector gives $P$ at $t=0$, while the coefficient of $t$ gives the normal direction. Multiplying all components of that direction by the same nonzero scalar would describe the same line.

Use the **product rule**: $\nabla(fg)=g\nabla f+f\nabla g$. Multiply each gradient by the other scalar function.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}
$$

(\ln{\left(x - y - 2 \right)} + 1)\mathbf i+(- \ln{\left(x - y - 2 \right)} - 1)\mathbf j

$$
